MAGGIE'S GRAVE. Au rambled through t' churchyard to-day, When o' wer' quate an' still, ' 4' An' t' cheery smell o' t' new-mown hay I Coom wafted off yon hill: An' t' summer breeze sung low to t' trees A song as wet mi e'en, For sooary thowta went through ml rapid Bi Maggie's grave so green. Poor Maggie waur a bonny lass, Her face wer' fresh an' breet,, Her voice we' like a layrock's song— So. gentle and so sweet; Her heart wer' true, her e'en wer' blue, Her laugh wer' leet an' gay, When to an' fro her daily toil 800 used to trip away. There coom a handsome roving lad, As won her simple heart, An' vowed through o' her life to bear A true an' monlv part. When love fost linked tbad life vvi' his , Heaw happy hoo did feel; 800 trusted one hoo'd never tried, An' loved her lad too weeL For Ned, when he wer' cooartin' her, Could varra plainly see Her love would fondly screen his fotes, Wodever they mut be: An' sooa, like mony a scamp beside, When t' weddin day wer' gone, He changed his tune, an' showed his-se A heartless, selfish men. What's leetly won is leetly loved Bi mortals here below; Thad lesson Maggie lived to learn I' loneliness an' woe: Ned went away wi' reckless mates A' drinkin' every fleet, While hoo lee waitin' wearily To hear his wanderin' feet. 800 hed a little comforter— A cherub fro' aboon ; Bud, weakly, like id feyther's love. Id vanished just as soon. An' when they laid her child i' t' grave Hoe knew her race wer' run; An' faded same as dayleet fades Just after t' settin' sun. Her heart wer' brocken, sure enough,- 600 a t' doctor sed his-sel' ; But when Ned's axed wed ailed his wife He says he ne'er could tell. Ah ! when age an' sickness come, They'll oppen t' wanderer's e'en, While conscience shows him wod id waur As filled yon grave so green! G. H. WALTON.

THE DREDGER.—As three men were watching the dredger at work in the river at South Benwell, one was heard to say, "Luik boo she's howkin' the dry muck cot off the wetter !" Say," said Berkey to his wife yesterday at dinner, "you didn't say anything to any one about what I was telling you night before last, did-you ? That's a secret." "A secret ? Why I didn't know it was a secret," she replied, kind of regretfully. "Well, did you tell it? I want to know." "Why no, I never thought of it since. I didn't know it was a secret." A CLEVER Peru..—ln the district of Heworth,s short time ago, several workmen were discussing the subject of intellectual acquirements. A man named John, who, it appears, is a noted boaster, remarked," Aal aa knaa as got by me rum studyin'. The skyul-maistor cud nivvor git me farthor than the pairt iv the bulk wheor Jack fell in the pond." " Whaat a pity," said another, " thoo wasn't like Jack, an' wes stuck thor yet!" TFIE DOCTOR'S ORDERS.—A young man, who lives not far from Byker, got his hand badly hurt the other day at his work, and was ordered by his doctor to refrain from taking any drink until it g t better. But as Tom liked a drop of geed beer, the prohibition went "against the grain." On one of his mates going into a bar he saw Tom standing with his glass in front of him, as usual. "Hallo, Tom," said he, "as thowt the doctor ordored tilos" not te drink oney mair boor wi' that sair hand." " Nevthor as de," said Tom, " aa's drinkin' wi' t'other hand !" SIDING WITH THE ANAECHISTS.—Jones : "Hello Brown, what is the matter with your eye ?" Brown (sadly): "Jim White fetched up there on all fours." Jones: "Yes, So it appears. What wag the cause ?" Brown: "Well, you see, I learned that he had accused me of siding with the anarchists, and the more I thought it over, the more I thought he lied. Finally I became convinced that he I was a liar' and broke the news to him gently, as he is subject to heart disease. But he was so Startled that he made a clean leap of five feet, and both feet and both fists struck me in the eye." Dvnso LIKE A GENTLEMAN.—One of the most interest- ing incidents of the late war is told by General Lytle, just before he received his fatal wound at Chickamauga. Be had made his brilliant charge into the midst of the enemy, where all chances of retreat were cut off. Sud- denly he thrust his hand into his coat Docket, drew forth a pair of kid gloves, and began putting them on. Asked by an aid the reason for this movement, so. unexpected, under such thrilling circumstances, the, general An- swered: "Don't you see we are surrounded, and that there are but two alternatives left us—to die or sur- render? For my part I propose to die like a gentle- man." He drew on his gloves and soon afterwards fell. Those who knew General Lytle in Cincinnati knew him to be most punctilious about the appointments of a gentleman, but no one ever supposed him capable of such incomparable coolness. THE ELEPHANT AND ass HYENA.—An elephant and a hyena being stationed near each other in a menagerie, the former took it upon himself to rebuke his brother in captivity. "You ought to cultivate a more amiable dis- position, said he. "Do you not observe how agreeable lam under all circumstances? This makes me a general favourite." "That is all very well," replied the hyena. "It is easy enough to be agreeable when you are fed with peanuts and candy from morning until night." "That has nothing to do with it," interrupted the elephant. "I should be pleased and affable if I received no more attention than you do. Do you see this boy appreaching with a package of candy? Observe my affAbility." The boy stepped to the elephant and offered him a chocolate cream drop, neglecting to mention that it was stuffed with cayenne pepper. The animal accepted it gracefully, but in less than a minute he was uttering a series of blood-curdling oaths, and otherwise conducting himself, in a highly reprehensible manner, so that his keeper had to come and remonstrate with him. .6 Humph!" muttered the hyena with a cynical smile, "it isn't well to be too blamed sure of one's amiability under all circumstances. Moral—Such is life. Sim:mixer A Scarcriaten.—The following is from an old journal :—A nobleman at Paris asked Lady R— why it was in general remarked abroad by foreigners that the Scotch who travelled were men of parts and learning, -while the English were generally wanting in both? Her ladyship, with her usual-vivacity, replied that only fools went out of England; but for Scotland, none but fools would stay in it. A Scotch nobleman, neither famous for parts or learning, Lord —, observed that her lady- ship was right with regard to the Scotch; for, says he, there are offices established in Scotland where every Scotchman must apply for a passport ere he can leave the country, and previous to the granting thereof he is examined with regard to his intellects and education, which, should they not arrive at the standard fixed for each, no passport is granted; but be is sent back for improvement; on a second application, the same form is observed; but should he apply a third time, and then be found wanting, he is remanded back for life. By this, says his lordship, your ladyship will plainly see none but I men of sense and learning can legally leave this country. ' " Then," replied her ladyship, 'rm sure your lordship was smuggled." This gave me .1 much more liberty to follow my principal occupation, 1 which, not to put too blunt a point on it, was hardly one which would have commended itself to the disciples of Sir Wilfred Lawson. Of course I pocketed the,greater portion of the earnings: . After working some of the southern counties, and meeting with many ludicrous adventures, we agreed to go north; and after a week or two found ourselves in Scotland. We had landed our- selves in a difficulty, for we found that the authorities would not allow us to stand in the markets of either Edinburgh or Glasgow, and we were soon in very low water. . One night we were in a small town still further north when my mate succeeded in getting a stand, and I went off to attend to other matters, I waited for my partner's return in vain; and I Went to look for him on the market, but could not find him. I ultimately dis- covered that he had sold stock-in-trade, goodwill, and everything for 25., and made tracks for parts unknown. 1 I hadn't a cent, the morning after, and I clicl not knqw which way to turn. My wits had never failed me up to now, and they didn't then. A thought struck me. I went and begged an old hat box from a shopkeeper, and I persuaded a joiner near by the place where I was lodging to give me some glue. I also procured a little string and some broken glass' and I commenced to make a weather indicator. I had no cat gut to work the figures with, but I got over that difficulty by rub- bing some glue over some common string and fixing "Jocky" and ".Enny" with that. I knew the thing would not work, but what could I do? Necessity knows no law. I tried to sell the indicator, but failed at several places. the price I asked for it being is. 61 At last rendered desperate, I went to the house of a magis- trate in the town I was in and offered him the article. I was asked to show my hawker's license and did so; and then he said more in fun than in earnest I could see that the thing would not work, and I assured him earnestly that it would; and that I would guarantee it to be an excellent weather indicator. In the ! end I succeeded in disposing of it to him for one shilling, and I have often wondered since how he got on with it. The shilling quickly disappeared, and it was while wondering how I should procure my next that I noticed a big burly man enter the lodging house, who seemed to be particularly flush. I contrived to get into conversation with him, the upshot of it being that he offered me 2s. a day as a bill sticker. He was a quack in the pill line; and was in the habit of heralding his approach to any particular town by sticking small yellow bills upon every post and coign of 'vantage he could get at. / jumped eagerly at the offer, and after the importance of "sticking plinty av pashte " on had , been duly impressed upon me. REMINISCENSES OF THE ROAD; OR, DOWN ON HIS LUCK. By. A. GOBBIN. It might be imagined from the title, unless distinctly stated otherwise at the outset, that this article related the doings of a modern Dick Turpin. It does nothing of the kind. I have frequented Bar Majesty's highways as much as most men, but only for the peaceful pu of making my way from one town to shothir in thrrurse of my weary wanderings over the length and breadth of Great Britain. Fortune compelled me to take to the road, but not with the hope of filling an empty purse by forcibly depriving other people of their money. Shanks pony was my only means of conveyance; and my stock- in-trade consisted of nothing more dangerous than an old tin tobacco box, a knife much the worse for wear, and a few coppers. In plain English, I was down on my luck, and obliged to go on ,tramp. The numerous incidents of a life on the road I propose now to briefly describe. It matters not how I came to this sorry plight. Suffice it to say that on starting I was fairly well dressed, and was a strong and healthy man. I have long since abandoned the profession of a tramp; but let me add that the end of my experiences in that line found me without a shirt to my back; with a pair of boots, the uppers and soles of which seemed in imminent peril of dissolving partnership ; with a hat too dilapidated for a respectable scarecrow; with a swallow-tailed coat, one sleeve and one tail of which were almost entirely gone, not to mention other shortcomings of that never-to-be- forgotten garment; and a pair of trousers to which the English language is incapable of doing justice. I went on the road, as I have before stated, a strong man, but I left it broken in health, and nearly done for. It would occupy far too much space to describe all of interest that befel me, and the reader must therefore expect the relation of a few incidents only. One fine Spring morning, in a year not necessary to be mentioned, found me, with the stock-in-trade pre- viously enumerated, on the road to the popular seaside resort of Blackpool, whither, I saw, numerous other gentlemen of my persuasion were also bound. After a day or two's fruitless wandering about the town I got a job at a circus in which there was nightly a comic per- formance in which an extraordinarily clever donkey figured. This animal was a curiously shapen "critter." His head was that of an ass—by which I mean to cast no reflection upon his intelligence—but his hind quarters bore a striking resemblance to those of a camel. His forelegs had a curious bend in them, which seemed to indicate that he was of a pious turn of mind; and, ' strange to say, the hind pair had a similar weakness. I know it is against all the rules of a donkey's anatomy that this should be so; but then the animal in question was no ordinary Jackass. The clown had the "mani- pulation" of " Jehosh"—short for Jehoshaphat, which was the name the donkey rejoiced in—and it was part of the animal's duty when "touched up" by the clown to turn, rise on his hind legs, and go from him in true prize-fighting attitude. This never failed to bring down the house with a roar. I was the hind legs. A much smaller man did duty as the forelegs. There was nothing of a donkey about the figure in fact except the legs. Now, the "Honourable Billy "—as my mate was called ' by, his familiars—had once acted for six weeks as cash- taker at a sparring booth; and the distinguished posi- tion of forelegs was assigned him because of the inti- mate knowledge he was thus supposed to have gained of tha noble art of self-defence. This made him con- ceited and rather arrogant in his demeanour towards me. We had had one or two slight quarrels before, but one night matters were brought to a crisis. The circus was crowded, and the " Honourable " was in rather a bad temper. We walked into the ring, and went through part of the programim•A We had arrived at the sparring scene, when, for some reason or other,l aroused Billy's ire, and he gave me a kick in the shins. This was too much to bear quietly, and I went for him. The donkey seemed to be suddenly taken with a fit of the colic, for he was quickly doubled in a heap on the floor, and all four legs were seen to be flourishing around in a remarkably lively manner, while Billy's groans, as he was getting his head punched, seemed to point to the fact that " Jehoali " had some grave internal trouble. And so he had. The house took it as a part of the per- formance, and taught(' loud and • long; the attendants came to the rescue of the clown, and started to belabour us with whip-handles; but the poor old donkey's troubles were not assuaged until Billy and I tumbled out of the skin, the one with a pair of lovely black eyes, and the other with a bleeding nose. The house saw it all, and laughed louder than ever. The result was disastrous to the principals, for the manager, in giving us the order of the sack, blandly explained that to con- tinue to employ a Jackass given to perpetual fits of this , violent nature would eventually destroy his reputation as the purveyor to the public of an entertainment in ' which there were two hours of fun without vulgarity. Well, after this, I was out of work for a time. I tried to get an engagement at Raikes Hall is a Zulu, but they told me that my Irish accent was too pronounced. I might have got a job as the partner of an itinerant teetotal lecturer, but, as he delicately put it, my breath smelt too strong. At length I got, work as a tout to an eating-house, where neither of these characteristics were regarded as a disqualification. From six o'clock in the morning until eleven at night I described, to a very ap- preciative British public, the contents of my proprietor's extensive larder for the princely wage of 103. a week and all found—which, as a rule, meant the leavings of the table and any quantity of table beer, judiciously let down at the water-tap, with a commendable regard to the strength of my stomach and head. From six until eight I dwelt exhaustively upon the advantages of rum and coffee as an appetiser; from eight until ten I was at it with the charms of breakfast with ham and eggs as the principal plat. After that I was engaged until 'twelve o'clock in trying to induce customers to partake of sundry succulent snacks in which bread and sausage formed no 'unimportant part, and which some of our rougher Lancakre customers used to style "a forenoon baggin." From twelve until three I had quit an appe- tistng list of viands to proclaim. Tea was much like breakfast, and supper bore a strong resemblance to the before-mentioned " bag,gin." I don't know what would have become of me if I had stayed at this em- ployment long. I should probably have gone off my head, and have had to be sent to an asylum. Fortunately, before this consummation was arrived at the season was brought to a close, and I found myself one morning, after a right royal spree in which the funds I had accumulated had been dissipated, on the road again. I had twopence in my pocket, and how to get enough to pay for my dinner was the question. I resolved to tramp it to Preston; and as I was going along the highway I came to a shop in which I saw a number of thread bobbins exposed for sale. An idea struck me. I went into the shop, and asked the good woman behind the counter how she sold them, and she said a dozen for 4d. I bought half-a-dozen, and disposed of them at a half-penny each on the way to Preston. On arriving there I had therefore 3d. in my possession; but though it was nearly noon I could not think of spending my mall stock of money on a dinner, so I eagerly Bast about for a chance of increasing my funds. At length I saw Old Moore's Almanac for the coming year on sale at a large stationer's shop, and I went in end fieught half- a-dozen for 3d. I had a pretty smart appearance at this time, and I went to an hotel close by, and asked the good-natured looking landlady at the bar if she would allow me to dispose of my stock-in-trade in the house, and she kindly consented. I went into the parlour, which was well filled, and I began to palaver about the advantages of the almanacs I had for sale, placing special emphasis upon the fact that this was Roberts' edition. I didn't know Roberts from Adam, but the manner in which I pressed the name upon the attention of the company made it appear as if there was some special virtue in the name. The men in the room eagerly caught at the bait, and I quickly sold' all I had at a penny each, and there was still a demand for more. I assured the company that I had a large stock of them at the apartments I had taken in the town—fancy, apartments !—and I would shortly return with more. I hurried off to the stationer's and invested in sixpenny- worth ; and five of these I sold at the same public-house I started at. I went on, and worked the public-houses in the vicinity very assiduously, every time I sold out replenishing and doubling my stock at the stationer's. This went on until well into the afternoon, and until I had in fact netted several shillings. At length I de-

- thought, to injure her. I cannot parley with ,you, fort I do not not trust the ruffians you have brought with you. If you mean to attack the castle, send away the women, for though / shall aim only at men, I eannot answer for chances.--Vnsomr BERTRAM LORRAINE." Tracy's cheek grew livid; he ground his teeth, and tore the letter into fragments. "BOys I" he cried savagely, "the villain owns that Miss Desmond is a prisoner; he says he will spare no one—gire him no quarter !" .Did Tracy believe that Lorraine lied? No; but he knew now that Hyacinth Desmond loved him, and all that was good in him seemed to snap like a thread, and he did not scruple to still keep up the fiction that Hyacinth was an unwilling prisoner in the hands of an unscrupulous roue. "By heaven !" said Lorraine, grimly, as Hyacinth covered her face with e quick deep sob, "if Tracy Mansfield were not of yourkith, I would speedily choke that lie back whence it came with a bullet. He stood ready to fire as he spoke, and as the words left hts lips there was a wild howl from the mob below and a simultaneous rush at the gate, while severalmen ill the rear of the mob fired almost at random at the window, the bullets whizzing harmlessly past their • mark; but Lorraine did not fire recklessly. One after the other the six barrels'were discharged, and only one shot failed to take effect. Hyacinth could now better help her lover by reloading, an operation which she per- formed with a deftness and rapidity that evoked his admiration, handing him the double-barrelled revolver as soon as the "six shooter" was discharged, and even the loading of the six barrels was accomplished with sur- prising celerity. Faith ! " said he, "you must have been to California, or campaigning. Where did you learn to load so rapidly?" "I used to practise it,"- she answered, "I hardly know why, except for fun. Terry and I fired at marks, and tried which could reload the quickest. Vincent, is the gate yielding?" A. volley of shot deep groans, and wild yells answered her for a moment. Then Lorraine said— The gate will not stand such battering much longer; but beyond it is the door, and the fools are showing signs of yielding—they don't rcl;sh such a rain of bullets. Ha, Regan! a-prayer were better than a blow!" The prayer was never uttered—the blow never given. Regan reeled, shot to the heart, and fell fc;rward on his face, It is cruel work !" said 'Lorraine—and for the first time his firm lip quivered-c-" to have to shoot men who come to save you ratter than to murder me; but on the head of the man who, for his own base revenge, lied to them must their blood rest. Regan deserves his fate—but, perchance, not the madman who follows him ; yet—" He raised his hand—forth sprang the deadly n,e4senger, and the stalwart young fellow rolled over, almost at Tracy's feet. A deep heavy groan among the men,--a piercing shriek from the women. They looked at one another, and paused. The old feeling of superstition was in every man's heart. This Fnglishman's life was pro- tected by a charm; he dealt death with awful pre- cision, yet himself remained scatheless: many bullets , bad been fired and not one had so much as grazed him; while for almost every shot he sent a man's life paid forfeit. Alone he resisted more than a hun- dred, and the gate had not yielded yet; how many ' more must fall before that point was gained? and when it was gained the doors, would still offer' a stubborn resistance. Tracy, seeing the crowd waver, made an effort to rally them; but one man turned upon him almost fiercely-- ' Aisy for you, Misther Mansfield; the masther i spares ye, because ye're Miss Hyacinth's cousin. The spalpeen hasn't fired at ye once; why should the leader escape and the men be murthered ? Tracy turned white with passion he dared not show, but ere he could reply somebody shouted out— "Father Malone, the priest, is comin'." And, over the moorland. gesticulating as he advanced, rode Father Malone at a swift galop. Hyacinth clasped her hands with almost a sob. "Oh, thank Heaven !" burst from her, "he may stop -this bloodshed." Lorraine drew the girl to his side and just touched his lips to her brow. "I would I could have spared them, dear one," he whispered. "I did not blame you, Vincent, you know that; the loss of life is at the men's own door, and Tracy's. I 'will never speak to hini again, as sister or friend.' Father Malone halted, breathless, and lifting his hand enforced silence. ' "What is all this?" he said, sternly, turning straight to Maasfield. "Do Ina you. Mr. Mansfield, a gintle- man, who should know betther, leading these poor people to commit ,nturther, an' lose their lives like sheep? An' ye don't know afther all that Hyacinth Desmond is kept there against her will." Tracy rode up to the speaker. "See here?" he said, , through his teeth, "do you think she .would go there of her own accord? She told me herself she disliked the man—she—" "Howl(' !"interrupted the rriest, " Vincent Lorraine is a bad man, X know; but mayn't be as bad as you think him. Anyway it wasn't for you to hound these poor people on to lose their lives, an' more. I belave that they'll have sinti for the constables." "Who has sent for them? Terence O'Conor ?" • "Why not? he'd think to rescue Hyacinth, an' de- pind on it 'tis no wan else; an' it'll go hard with ye that ye've taken the law into•. yet own hands, Misther Mansfield." The priest said this with a significant glance. Tracy retorted recklessly—" I care nothing. I have nothing now to live for but revenge." " Ye're as wicked as the man yonder," said the priest, severely, "but I'll have no more bloodshed if I can pre- vent it." He turned away and rode in among the people." Bhoys, listen to me. Ye'll not get into that house till the half av ye is killed, an' not then, maybe. The constables have been sint for—Silence !—an' it'll be a noice rickoning thin; but maybe things are not as bad as ye think. I'll not belave Misther Lorraine would irate Hyacinth Desmond any way unbecoming a gin- tleman— " We'll have him out, and we'll have his life!" shouted a number ot the men. Grady loudest of all. " Howld yer tongues I" cried the priest, angrily, "an' you, Dermot Grady—it wasn't to save Hyacinth Des- mond that you an' some others came here, I know. Bhoys, I'm goin' to snake to Mr. Lorraine." He rode close up to the gate and called out Lorraine's' name, and Lorraine called back— " Climb the wall and drop into the court, and I will admit you. But first guarantee that the men hold their hands." That will L" returned the priest. " Bhoys," turn- in" again to the mob, "rm going into the castle to shr'pabe with Misther Lorraine—" "Whist ! father, the spalpeen will shoot ye I" cried a woman. "Shame on,ye, Msll Corrigan," said Father Malone, sternly, "to think any inm, aann, wy•eudlndnostthpartomtriasietomesl tell ye, edteheadt. Iwhile f'm gomne no man will lift a band against the gate." " We promise!" they all cried, and the priest knew no one would dare to break it. Besides, the people did not•care to sacrifice any more life if they could help it, and they thought they saw in Lorraine's offer a disposi- tion to make terms. The mounting .of the wall was a rather comical pro- .. ither

have not seen your mother; but they tell me that when you were missed, she went up to-Clanmorris. Hyacinth; Hyacinth, ho* come ye here?" ' The girl flushed crimson. "Do you think," she said, drawing back, "that he brought me here, or that I was persuaded to Omer-raid he not tell you?" ' • She looked at Lorraine. He shrugged his shoulders. "I thought Father Malone had better hear it from you, Hyacinth.'" ' • • "Hyacinth !" The priest glanced quickly from one to the other; but suffered the girl to lead hirn to a seat, and then she knelt down before him, and briefly told him all—how she had watched the men; hOw she 'had discovered the conspiracy, and how she had fled to Curramore to warn its lord of his peril. In deepening wonder the priestlistved, Lorraine standing by silent the while, leanin,,t against the wall with folded arms; and when -Hyacinth• ceased, Father Malone laid his hand on her head, and his voice shook as he said,." Child, ye are • a heroine—a brave, noble' I girl,' afid yer mother an' yer counthry will be proud of Lye'. Misther Lorraine, pardon me that I wronged you; but behave me, sir, I, never thought as badly of ye as . perhaps some of these ignorant men thought." - "I ought to be grateful for so much, Father Malone," replied Lorraine, with some irony. "Tracy Mansfield —allow me to add—might have spared some blood- shed, or at least tried to do so; for I sent him a mes- sage that Hyacinth had come here to warn me of the plot to,assassinate me; and he choose to regard that message as a lie." t. "On his head," said the priest, rising hastily, "may the curse of Heaven rest! Misther Lorraine, I belave that Misther O'Conor has sent for the constables, but I can make the -people go home if ye'll make them a few promises." "I will not make one, Father Malone. Against those who came here under the idea that I was forcibly detaining Hyacinth Desmond I will not lift my hand. fam sorry I had to shoot any orthem'; but those of the murderers who survive must reap as they have sown, and any man who from this time continues the strife shall be made to suffer. From this position nothing shall make me swerve. Moreover, as you will know, concession would not purchase safety. My life would be as surely taken as if these men had com- plete possession of the castle at this moment." . "Too thrue !" said the priest, sighing; his last hope fell as he saw that Hyacinth had no intention of in- terceding. " IlYacinth," he said, after a moment's pause, " will you let me take yon to your mother? Your life is safe —especially with me." But Hyacinth, flushing to her brow, shrank back to Lorraine 's side, and he smiled and passed his arm round her, drawing her close to him. "Hyacinth," he said, gently, "act freely—as your own heart dictates; you will be safe—Father Malone need not tell these people the truth." "I• would not shelter under the lie," returned the girl, passionately,," and if I would, I could not leave you -now. Tell ler Father Malone, tell mother what you have heard, and that I will come to her soon. Or stay-1 will write a message, and one of the boys, I know, will take it." "An' will ye tell her, child," said the priest, more sorrowfully than sternly, "that you've given your heart where she'll never let you give yer hand, unless ye mane to fly in yer mother's face, an' yell never do that. Hyacinth." ' "I don't know, said Lorraine, with a decided touch of hauteur, "that that question need be tntered upon now. The matter that brought you, father, being settled, perhaps you Mu take some refreshment while Hyacinth writes." "I thank you, Misther Lorraine, no," returned the priest, as Hyacinth turned to the table to write. "You will not eat of my salt or drink of my cup!' said Lorraine indifferently. "Well, as you will. A man who seeks his own is an outcast in Connaught; but take heart of grace, I shall not remain much, longer in the land. The bullet Las been arbitrator between my tenants and me, though not quite as they intended." The letter was written, and Father Malone retired, mounting the wall by moans of a small ladder which Margaret placed for the purpose, and instantly with- drew when he had descended on-the other side. Then waving aside the crowd, which clamoured around him, the priest approached Tracy, and spoke in a low,,stern tone, " Misther Mansfield, ye'll well. to take yerself off; ye'ye• been treacherous for yer own revinge, an' made these poor people shed their blood. If I tell them the thruth, some av em'll not be kept off av ye so be wise, and escape while ye can." Tracy hesitated one moment; but hp saw that re- monstrance or 'excuse was useless, and setting 'his teeth he turned his ,horse's head and rode rapidly away. Father Malone then harangued the mob, exhorting them to disperse. It was not true, he. said, that Mr. Lorraine had carried off Hyacinth Desmond; she 'had discovered a plot to murder the lord of Curramore, and had gone to the castle to warn him. In the midst of' the tumult which this communication raised, Father Malone gave Hyacinth's letter to a lad, and bade hirn make all speed to Clanmorris and give it to Mrs. Des- mond. A diversion was Caused by the sudden appear- ance of a horseman rapidly approaching over the moor- land, and almost as the shout arose, "Misther O'Conor," Terence, hot and breathless, drew rein. • "Saints In Heaven !" he exclaimed, "what' bloody work is this? Are you Irishmen—are you men, who seek one man's life? If you are wise, clear off while lon can. Silence, and hear use !" He lifted his hand. "Silence!" roared the priest, and "the order was obeyed. In a loud clear voice O'Conor added— ' • Within an- hour there will' be a body of con- stabulary—twelve armed men—from Roscommon. Within two hours a company of rldiers, from Galway." The war-like spirit of the men had been evaporating rapidly under Lorraine's terrible rain • of bullets. OConor's information put the finishing touch; and a great cry arose, while men and 'women gathered round the young soldier, exclaiming--" Ye'll not inform, Misther O'Conor, yell not inform 7" Go to your homes," was O'ConorPs reply, "and I'll forget many a face I know well. Boys, r know some of you at least only wanted to save Miss Hyacinth; but you had no right to think of murder; you had no right to think Mr. Lorraine deserved death. 'Tis tic) lie I told you, Terence O'Conor never yet lied to aty man." ' "Children," cried the priest, "if ye stay here therehl no more bloodshed. Hyacinth Desmond don't nebd yer rescuing, an' yell not kill Misther Lorraine while I shtand by; besoides, look here "—pointing to the corpses—"ye'll dhrop wan by wan. Disperse while ye can, but if ye shtay I'll denounce every, man av ye .from the altar, whether the military take ye or not." • Father Malone folded his arms and loOk6d what he meant. The men looked at each other—at the priest r-at Terence O'Conor—at the castle—and a deep, heavy groan ran among them Like the moaning noise that goes before the whirlwind on the deep, and one voice exclaimed alond:— " We're done now, because the sodgers are comin', out be all the powers above let Misther Lorraine guard -his cursed loife, for it isn't worth that"--dashing' a stone to the ground—" an' I don't belave the lie that Hiss Hyacinth found out we was goin' to kill him. He wik her off, an' he shall die for that; an' for his hard- ness, an' for these bhoys he's murdhered." "Dr -lot Grady." -aid the -'st, sternl: toll be

HARVEST FESTIVALS. • ALL SAINTS CHURCH, ,THELWALL. On Saturday and Sunday harvest thanksgiving services were held in the above church. The sir- vices were held on Saturday at 7-30 p.m, and on Sunday'at 8-30 a.m., 10-30 a.m., 3 p.m., and 6-30 p.m. The preacher on Saturday evening 'was the Rev. C. C. Elcum. M.A., vicar of St. Agnes, Liver- pool ;on Sunday morning the Rev: J. J. Langham, M.A., principal of St. Elphin's, occupied the pulpit; in the afternoon, the Vicar; and in the evening the Rev. L. J. T. Darvrall, 8.D., vicar of Walton. The church, as usual, was very tastefully decorated. The services were all well attended, and particularly that of Sunday evening. The anthem, " Fear not, 0 land," by the Rev. Mr. Darwall, of Walton, was sung. The tenor solo" was taken by Mr. Westbrook, of Holy Trinity choir. The offertories amounted to over .E 34 and are to be divided between the Dio- cesan Charities and the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel. THE REFORMED CHURCH OF ENGLAND. On Sunday harvest thanksgiving services were held in. Emmanuel Church, Bold-street, Warring- ton, when special sermons were preached by the Rev. F. L. Good, who took for his text in the morning Lev. xxiii. 11 and 12, and in the evening Jer. viii. 20.. In the afternoon there was a children's service, when an address was given on the word "Manna." There were good congregations at each , service. BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.

On Monday,a race that promised to be one of the most interesting that have been decided in the annals of pedestrianism was announced to take place at Lillie Bridge. The competitors were H. Hutchins, of Putney (who has held the short distance professional champion- ship for several years, and holds the tecords at 140 yards, 200 yards, 300 yards, and 350 yards), and H. Gent, of Darlington, who has recently won two Sheffield £lOO i handicaps n such time that he was thought worthy of being pitted against the holder of the title. The match was to run 120 yards for £2OO and the cham- pionship, and as both had received a careful pre- paration and were pronounced by good judges to be in grand condition, an exciting contest was anticipated. The day, too, was favourable, and quite 5,080 spectators assembled at 'West Brompton to witness the sport. At first odds of sto 2 were laid on Gent, who being much the younger man, was greatly fancied, but as the time advertised for the start (five o'clock) drew near, there was a disposition to back the ether, and after taking shorter odds the betting veered round to such an extent that the public began to suspect something was wrong, and when ultimately extravagant odds were offered on Hutchens it became evident that the race would not be decided on its merits, and the spectators began to be uneasy. The men were then disrobing in the dressin,e-room.but seemed a long while coining out. The ' public, however, knowing that these events are generally held back as late as the light will permit, for pecuniary reasons, waited patiently, but at length 'lt leaked out that both runners had decamped and that there would be no race. At ,first this was either disbelieved ,or ' net realised, but when it was placed beyond all doubt a scene of unprecedented confusion occurred. 4ailings and gates were broken down, and, having no one to wreak their vengeance on, the mob started wrecking the place, being evidently, de- termined to have their money's worth out of somebody, as naturally it was impossible to refund each person his money, a process that would have occupied hours. The first thing to go was the high partition near the gym- nasiutn. The wreckers then tare down the palings by the railway, and swarmed over the lines.. An ugly rush was theremacle for the centre of the course, the wooden rails offering feeble resistance. The telegraph-board was quickly smashed into pieces, the flagstaff was torn; down, and then the long shed by the Sea,greave-road was attacked, and soon only the corrugated iron roofing and Its supports remained. The 'police, of whom there was, as usual, only a limited supply, were uttefly powerless ' to cheek the progress of the riot, and wheareinforce- - the

PRANCE.--SCIiiOOLBOY soLDAßs.—.r.svAit, EPIDEMIC. --ROYALIST PRINCES.—DE- CI,ARATIOU BY GENERAL BOI7LANGER. Paws, SATIIII'LIAY.—A novel sight was witnessed in Paris this morn Ing, when an enthusiastic crowd of some 10,000 persons /gathered at the gate of La Chapelle to 'welcome a delsachment of 150 schoolboy soldiers who had taarched frotn.Amiens at the average rate of 15 miles a !lay. After the Mayor of the district had harangued the lads, they marched, amid the cheers of the assembled crowds, to the Avenue Tradaine, where they were re- 'viewed bye General leanningros. The little boys were hos- pitably entertained during the journey. The lads will remain, at the College of Chaptal while in Paris, and then trudge bads. Paws, SIINDA.T.—There is another typhoid epidemic, 'due to the substitutioa during the recent long spell of hot dry weather of the water of 'the Seine for spring i water n many quarters of Paris. On the Ist of September there were 353. typhoid-stricken patients in the hospitals. There are now 509. The number of those who_are treated in their homes is said to be very great. The facts that! state should not frighten visitors away, as the late heavy rains have renewed the spring water Supply. A telegram !rem Paris says it is staled by one of the mormne papers that on the meeting of the Chamber motions wirl be made for the-expulsion of all the Princes of the Orleans and Bonaparte families, and the confisca- tion of their property. Sr. GALMIER (LOIRE), SIINDAT.—The manceuvres of the lath Army Corps, of which General Boulanger is the commander, ended yesterday in a general engagement, about four miles to the north of this place, between the 25th and 26th Divisions. To-day the troops were re- viewed by 'General Boulanger, who, before the -march- past, made a speech to the officers. , Criticising the , --operations of the day before, the General praised the dash of the men, but urged most strongly on the officers 'the necessity of giving-wider exercise to the offensive :tacticsawhich were proper to the French army. He coo- cluded with the following words:—" We have to-day more need than ever of the qualities of the warrior. ' ! the hour has not yet struck for the disarmament If 'the peoples of Old Europe. lt.is madness to believe it; it is a crime to say it, for it points to peace at any price as the goal to which the country should aspire; and <err -enemies, who often appraise us at ourreal value better than 'we do ourselves, know- very well that we have not gotsci fax as that. More Than ever, then, we must continue to -work. It is for France."

Orders have been issued from the War Office to the effect that all cavalry regiments are to be armed with the latest pattern of the Blordenfelt machine gun. A. brutal fight took place at Adswood, just outside the borough of Stockport, on Saturday, between a Stockport man and an individual from Poynton. The fight lasted about an hour, and was of a most feroci.ms character, the combatants, it is stated, using feet as well as fists. There were about 100 spectators present, but the affair had been kept so quiet that the police did not get wind of it till it was over.

ELOPEMENT AND Biramy.—At Huddersfield, on Monday, Wilson Heywood, yeast dealer, was committed for trial on a charge of bigamy. His first marriage to Elizabeth Cicely Winntook place at St. John's Church, Wakefield, in 1859, following an elopement. They. parted, and the prisoner, in 1886, went through the marriage ceremony at Ramsdemstreet Congregational Church, Huddersfield, with Sarah Jane Booker. He described himself as a widower.

One of the bullets lodged in the nee and two in the breast, her injuries being cf a serious nature. Directly afterwards the young man fired into his own mouth, and big wounds were of such a nature that no hopes are entertained of his recovery. Mer- cer had worked for Robertson's father, who is a hairdresser at Southwark, but he left when the father objected to the e4uttship between him and his daughter. The girl had gone tO Pew her lover a visit on Monday, and he shot her as stated ihn the PreBenCe of his sister. The drawers and cupboards in the house had beeu ransacked, and about ES in money stolen. The woman states that imme- diately after the departure of her husband for his work, a tramp, wearing blue spectacles and a slouch hat, knocked at the door and asked for a drink of water, and on her turning to procure one she vras overpowered and tied in WO manner described.

'THE RAILWAY', -.AtOIL/SNT DONCASTER .- 24 KILLED'. AND 68 INJURED. • MESSAGE .FRONI THE QUEEN. The number of 'persons who have' ost-their lives from Injuries received in the appalling calamity-which occurred shortly after noon on Friday, at Hekthorpe,— no mile from Doncaster, on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shireßailway, now reaches 24, and it is unfortunately more than probable that one or two other names may have to be added to the death-roll. As was stated on Saturday. 16 persons were killed instantaneously in the collision, and three others succumbed to their fearful injuries I shortly:atter the accident took place. The bodies were I removed to the mineral offices, a short distance from the scene of the disaster, where two rooms were set apart for their reception, and during the course of the afternoon four of the victims were identified. Groups of people in search of missing friends continued to visit I the temporary mortuary at intervals on Friday night and Saturday, and by five o'clock on Saturday afternoon all the dead had been identified, with one exception, that of a man whose body presented a ghastly sight, the head having been fearfully smashed, and the face crushed beyond recognition. He had also been disembowe,lle& and the clothes formed the only clue to identification. The remains were afterwards found to be those el Arthur Mitchell, Sheffield, whose wife was also killed. Several of the other bodies were also recognised by the clothing or by articles found upon them. Some had their faces battered fiat, legs and arms broken, and great bruises upon their bodies. One body has been nearly cut in two, and another was a mass of disfigured flesh. Painful scenes were witnessed when husband or wile recognised the mutilated remains of those who were dear to them, and the shock was all the greater when it was found that a husband who was supposed to have been at work in Sheffield, and who had intended to spend a holi- day unknown to him wife at Doncaster races, had met ac untimely death in a man uer se tragic Mr. Henry Middle. too, of Sheffield, has lost his wife and child. 'He ban been to 'Doncaster during the week driving a conveyance. and his wife had arranged to go over by. the excursion train and accompany him home. When he received in• formation of the accident he proceeded to Elexahorpes in :search of his wife. Returning in the evening he saw Ihe bodies in the dead-heuse, and tecognisedl.l;at of his wife with her baby, boy lying in her lap. The Pribr man utterly broke down, and for some tireecould not tell the police the names and ages of his loved ones. At last, as he looked on the body of Mrs. Middleton, he said. "Ay. _ 'tbr

He did riot see any caution s*nal exhibited from Ileaqiorpe signal- box. He was -going at 35 miles an hour when he first saw the Midland train. Steam was off at the time, and he at once applied the vacuum brake. The fireman opened the sand-valves and put on the tender hand brake. Witness was looking ahead all the time, and saw the Midland train as soon as it was possible to do so. He saw no flag signals, hut admitted that he was not particularly looking for flag signals. When the colli- sion occurred he did not think his train was going at more than twelve mites an hour. The inquiry was adjourned. THE INQUEST. The County Coroner resumed his inquiry on Tuesday, and said that Sir Z. Watkin, the Chairman of the !Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, Railway Company, wished to make a statement, which would probably much facilitate their labours. Sir E. Welkin said he could only repeat what had been already said as to the sorrow and grief the directors felt at this sad aCcideet. It was not for him in say way to aeticifate what the inquiry :they were about solemnly to enter upon would result in: bu t, in order to save trouble and reassure some Of the poor people interested, he wished to say, on behalf of himself and his colleagues, that it was not the Inten- tion of the directors to dispute the liability of their com- pany. • He wished Slumber to say that those who met them in a just spirit would be dealt with quickly, and be hoped satisfaeterily. The evidence of the railway men was proceeded with, Sit E. Watkin and ether oftimals retiring. . Edward Beerskill. the clerk in charge of the Hexthorpe ticket pfatforan, said that the Midland train Carrie op at 12 13, and two minutes afterwards he heard the Liverpool and Hull train coming lap. He heard the application of the vacuum brake, and the train immediately struck the near end of the Midland van, and telescoped into two carriages!' immedietely traffic was stopped in every direction Nmeteen persons died immediately after being extricated from the carriages. The order was that \ the tickets of bhl ordinary trains should be examined at flexthorpe .on Wednesday and Friday. but they were not collected on the 325 Liverpool and Hull train on Wed- nesday,, but at Cenisboreegb. Robert Davis, fireman on the M. S. and L. train, ! whose evidence was not taken on Monday, said . that en 'Friday he was the, 'fireman for Taylor. He bad 'been eight years in the service. Altus the train left Tenistone they had eleven carriages At Hexthorpe 'Junction they were checked; the signal was against them, and the home signal also at danger' ! At that time the train was travelling at the rate Of 15 to ,20 miles an hour. Steam was shut off when they got ; over the incline, and the brake applied half-way between the distant-signal and the home signal, and the speed was reduced to 10 miles per hour. They whistled for the home signal, and it was lowered. They proceeded with steam off past -the -junction, and saw no tag whatever. They had -not received any caution. After paasing the junction he_ssw the signal-off, and said it was all right The driver applied the steam a little, and shut it off shortly after 'for the gradient. At the time the speed was from 15 to '2O miles an hots, and no brakes were on between the junction and the ticket platform. Witness saw two men on his side of the road with flags. The first -was directly under the signal post, and the other about fifty yards on the junction side of the bridge: He saw no signal he could take from the first man: The man had both flags in one hand,and was gesticulating, but witness broad net tell what he was saying. He was not giving any sign that he was aware of. He was not holding a red flag out, nor waving it. He first saw him when he was pas. sing the signal, and could not say whether he had been wav- ing the flag before he got to him. tie had been looking for a starting signal He did not tell the driver he had seer, the man. After the accident he told him he had seen a second man. Be saw the second flag signalman when within a few yards of him. He was holding his flag out, and put one finger op. Witness took the latter for the danger signal. The man did not. call out. The train was then running from 10 to 20 miles an hour. Witness did not call out to the driver, because he had no time, as the driver had•then sighted the train at the platform. The driver sighted the- train immediately he passed the' second flagman. He said "Whoa" Witness opened the sand valves,and the driver applied the vacuum indicator. but the brake did not seem to act as- well as it might have done. The rails were greasy with rain corn- ing on. The driver reversed the engine and put the steam against it just before they came to the Midland train. The speed then would be between five and ten miles an hour. Witness was not hurt. Between the first and second flagmen he was looking ahead, but pot for flags. He did not know the block working was sus- pended. He bad had notice, but did not 'read that part.. He was under the impression that the tickets were taken at Conisborough, and did not know it. was the order thst on Wednesday and Friday all ticketsshould toe examined at the Hexthorpe Siding. He had not read that order. Both he and the driver were perfectly sober. Stanley, guard on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire train, said that the tickets were not taken at Conishornugh,ns they had instructions to collect them at Hexthorpe. Thos. Smith, inspector in the traffic department, who was travelling with the train, said that in coming through Hexthorpe junction he saw two men with flags—one waving violently. The driver must have known of the instructions. He expected to stop at Hexthorpe, and saw a green flag waved at the' junction box and after- wards the flagmen waving red flags violently. The train passed them at fifteen or 20 miles an hour, and he noticed no efforts to check. The brake was not applied, or he must have felt it. The Coroner adjourned the inquiry until Tuesday next. The jury propose before resuming to visit the scene of the accident, and the portion of the line where the block system was suspended, as several jurymen have ex- pressed doubt whether the driver could have a clear view of the eround signalmen. The Borough Coroner of Doncaster on Wednesday opened his inquiry into the cause of death of the five victims of the Hexthorpe collision who died in the Infirmary. He was assisted by Major Marindin, Board of Trade inspector, who had made another inspection of the scene of the dis- aster. Witnesses were examined to show that the regula- done were issued to all the drivers and firemen. Davis, the fireman, was called, but, under advice, refused to say wbv Le did not read the instructions or to answer further ques- tions; and Taylor, the driver of the train which ran into the Midland train, having been cautioned, declined to give evi- dence. Mr. Young, solicitor to the Midland Company, said they received a copy of the regulations, and the driver of the Midland train was specially selected for duty because be knew the working on these occasions. The inquiry was ad- journed till next day. On Thursday the Doncaster Borough Coroner resumed his inquiry into the deaths which occurred at the Infirmary as a result of the Hexthorpe collision. Several officials of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Com- pany were present, and accompanied the jury in an inspec- tion of the line at and beyond Hexthorpe. A number of witnesses were examined, but their evidence was substan- tially the same as that whicn has been given at the Board of Trade inquiry. The Coroner, in summing up, said it was clearly established that very good arrangements were made for working the traffic, and if thoee arrangements had been carried out the collision would not have occurred. It appeared to him that both the driver and stoker of the Manchester, Sheffield., and Lincolnshire train had neglected to observe the regulations given to them for their guidance. The jury found that the five deceased persans lost their lives by the collision, which was caused by the negligence of Tay- lor, the driver, and Davies, the fireman, of the Sheffield train, whom they found guilty of manslaughter. The two men were ar-rested in the room, and will be brought -before the magistrates.
SARAH BERNEIARDT'S IMMENSE RECEIPTS • AND PATTI'S PERIL

_ Sarah Bernhardt's receipts, for her late tour in South America, are the largest ever taken by any dramatic artiste. But the reckless Sarah scarcely ever has a franc to spare! Patti has also achieved great success, and a very largs amount of money, in Mexico and South America, but came very near being the victim of a dynamiter who attempted to throw an explosive bomb at her while she was singing at the Grand Opera House in San Francisco, California. She was called again and again in front of the curtain when, as she was finally retiring, a man in the gallery suddenly rose, picked up a bomb from under the seat, and raising it in the air, was about to throw it, when it exploded In hie hand, shattering his arm and face, and inflicting other injuries. Had the man not placed himself under the protection of a policeman, who met him as he was rushing down stairs, he would have been torn in pieces by the in- furiated people. Patti displayed great coolness and pres- ence of mind, and succeeded in restoring quiet by singing Home, Sweet Home." Poor Patti! It is a wonder she was not killed by the nervous shock, or that she did not faint, or that her hair did not turn gray through fright. Think of Patti with gray hair! A beautiful head of hair is the crowning glory of woman, and its loss is her greatest misfortune—a mis- fortune which may be prevented by the use of that famous hair restorer and dressing, known as Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will prevent baldness and restore gray hair to its natural color, strength and gloss. ,1 It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the civilized world.

Mr. WILLIAM BIAGDIN, of Edensor, Blakewell, Derby- shire, was a sufferer from sciatica for two years. St. Jacobs Oil completely cared him when all other remedies had failed. Six miners employed in the West Cannock Colliery, Staffordshire, were severely injured by an explosion of gas I in the workings on Thursday morning. It is feared that in two cases the injuries will prove fatal. The eight prisoners charged with being concerned in the Moonlighting outrage near Lisdoonvarna, when Head-con- constable Whelehan was murdered, were again brought up at Ballyvanghan on Thursday, and further remanded. A Lloyd's telegram from Melbourne says the Derry Castle bound from Geelong for London, was totally wrecked on the Auckland Islands on March 20. Only eight per- sons were eaved, and these have been lauded at Mel- bourne. JAPANESE Goons at London Prices, MAYOR A CO.. 175, Oxford.etreet, Manchester.-1.8. The Finest Terra Ootta (for painting on) in the market at half the usual charges.— '
GENERAL NEWS. •

English tourists will be glad to learn that the English Government has issued a circular ordering Custom House officers to be more polite to travellers. Lady Houghton, of Fryston Hall, near Pontefract, died on Monday afternoon at Lord Crewe's residence at Crewe, vlffitther her ladyship had gone to be out of the way of fever, which had broken out at Fryston.

In compliance with a memorial from the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, an order in Council has been issued authorising them to issue additional Bank of England notes to the amount of £450,000. The last order, authorising an issue to the extent of £750,000, was made in 1881. _ _ _

Robert Thompson, corn miller, of Leeds, made a des- perate attempt to murder his wife at Selby on Monday afternoon. They had been separated for some time, and on her refusing to return to Leeds with him, he cut her throat with a razor in three places. He was arrested. The woman is in a critical condition.

The Works Committee of the Brighton Town Council have approved of the plans for a new theatre in the King's-road, but an exception was taken on the ground that no provision had been made for an iron curtain. It was explained that the plans conformed to the bye-laws, and the Council had no option in the matter. Mr. J. W:Kirton, the well-known temperance author and lecturer, has been appointed the organising agent of the Provisional Committee of the new National Prohibi- tion party. He will during the autumn actively promote throughout the country the special business connected with the Prohibition Convention, to be held in London Court
cm December Ist. .diff P,
