At the Can..— face a man _ isher, glazier, Gough-street, has been committed for trial at the assizes on a charge of setting fire to his own house. At the time of the fire he was at Newport, his wife and three children being in bed. The children were got out of the house by a neighbour, but the wife had to jump from the bedroom window. Much excitement has been created at Riverside, Glam- organshire, by the elopement of the wife of a shipping clerk with a sea captain, who was residing with them. The pair took with them several valuable articles and sums of money belonging to the deserted husband, who is left with three young children. No trace has been found of the wandering couple.

Harry Coulson, landlord of the Wheat Sheaf Inn, Nottingham, and well known in the music-hall profession as a variety entertainer, committed suicide on Sunday. He had been suffering from consumption, and as his recovery was regarded as hopeless, he became greatly de- pressed, and he was found in bed with his throat cut and a razor lying by his side. _ _ _ .

Mr. georie -Forster, of Penzance, a member of the Rothschild Hunt, while driving home on Saturday night from a shooting party at Mr. B. T. Fountaine's, at Stoke Hammond, was thrown from his phaeton, the horse having bolted in the dark and brought the vehicle into collision with a mud heap. Mr. Forster's neck was broken by the fall, and he died immediately. A PrAtrilßLV FRENCHMAN.—Mr. Grande, merchant, Newport, Monmouthshire, has just been fleeced of £2OO. Meeting a Frenchman with a lavish display of jewelry, Mr. Grande invited him home. The Frenchman made love to his daughter. proposed marriage, and was ac- cepted. He said he had an estate in France he wished to dispose of, and asked Mr. Grande for a loan of £2OO. The latter innocently lent him the money, and the man decamped. Some sensation was caused in St. Thomas's Church, Stockport, on Sunday morning by the action of a woman. The rector, who was reading out the banns of marriage, had announced the name of a gentleman, and was about to mention the lady's name, when a woman rose in the aisle and said, "I forbid those banns." After the service the forbidder of the banns, who, we understand, is the mother of the lady in question, had an Interview with the rector. _

The only missing body connected with the Ilfracombe yacht disaster—that of Mr. James Hard, of Ewell, Surrey—was recovered on Saturday night on the rocks at the foot of the Torts Walks. It was found to be almost nude, and the sum of thirty pounds supposed to be in the trousers pockets VMS missing. The body of Mr. Harry Rayner, employed by Mr. R. 0. Davis, Porchester- road, London, was recovered five miles from Ilfracombe on Friday, and identified on Saturday. Over 1,000 persons assembled in front of Leicester Prison on Saturday to witness the release of a man named William Smith, of Thurmaston, who had under- gone seven days' imprisonment for declining to have his child vaccinated. The chairman and several members of the Leicester Town Council and Board of Guardians held a meeting opposite to the entrance to the gaol, and declined to disperse at the request of the police, the leaders of the meeting handing their cards to the police ha facilitate further proceedings should these be insti- stuted. _ _

FATAL CARRIAGE Accookrr.—On Sunday afternoon, as Colonel Cobbe., inspector of police, was being driven down High-street, Chelmsford, by Major Poyntz' chief constable of Essex, the horse bolted and dashed into the gateway of the Saracen's Heed Hotel. Colonel Cobbe was thrown out and rendered insensible, and an aunt and daughter of the hotel-keeper, who were crossing the yard at the time, were knocked down and severely in- Jured. The former succumbed to her injuries shortly afterwards, and the latter was on Monday night lying unconscious.

A man named Ernest Edward Jackson was, at the Central Criminal Court, on Saturday, sentenced to 12 months' hard labour for a very heartless fraud. He appears to have taken an office in Chancery-lane, and represented himself as an nuctioneer ana surveyor, though he did not hold an auctioneers license. Ile ad- vertised "immediate and permanent situations for clerks," mentioning £72 per annum as the salary, and requiring a deposit of £3O. In this way he received from applicants over £l,OOO. It was stated that there were more than 20 cases against the prisoner. TEE litsnor OV SODOR AND Mex.—Bishop Bardsley preached his first sermon in the north of the Isle of Man in St. Paul's Church, Ramsey, on Sunday night. The church, which will accommodate over 1,000 people, was crowded some time before the appointed hour for ser- vice, and, although additional seats were provided in the aisles and chancel, many were unable to obtain admis- sion. The Bishop preached from St. Mark, chapter xiii., verses 30 and 31, and powerfully advocated the claims of the Additional aerates Society, in aid of which the offertory was devoted, and to which there was a very liberal response.

ANOTIIII-12 FIR R AT EXETER.—EXCITING SCENES.-- On Saturday, two houses and their contents were destroyed bfr fire in Exeter. The outbreak was on pre- mises immediately opposite the ruins of the theatre, and the utmost excitement and alarm prevailed, as the fire spread with great rapidity. One invalid old lady was in great danger, and when two men went to her rescue, she objected to leave, beeause she was not dressed. They, without further ado, rolled her in a blanket and carried her downstairs. A man at the adjoining house had to escape by the window. Captain Shaw, who has been conducting the theatre inquiry, was present and directed the firemen, ALARMING FIRE IN LONDON: Two LIVES LOST.—About two o'clock on Sunday morning a destructive fire broke out at 274, Strand, premises recently opened as a hair- cutting saloon, and occupied by several families. The building was extremely old, and constructed to a great extent of wood. The flames spread with alarming rapidity. the whole facade of the house being speedily enveloped in flames. Considerable excitement was created by the appearance of some of the occupants shortly after the outbreak on the roof of the house and upon the arrival of a strong force of the Metropolitan Fire Brigade, in charge of several steam fire engines, they were rescued from their perilous position and conveyed to a place of safety. Two sons of Mr. Serne, hairdresser (John, aged 13, and Leo, 10), were burned to death. Notwithstanding the efforts of the firemen, the house hi which the fire originated was completely gutted, and the adjoining premises (Asten's Hotel) were considerably damaged by fire and water.

SHIPPING DISASTERS.—GREAT LOSS OF LIFE; The Cunard steamer ::;ervia, which arrived at Queens- town on Saturday from New York, brought intelligence of the capsizing of the French fishing scheoner Cordelia, on the Grand Banks, and the loss of her crew of 16. Despatches from St. John's, Newfoundland, report that the French fishing vessel St. Pierre, had been passed bottom up, and it was feared that, her crew of 15 men were drowned. According to a telegram from Silt Cove, Labrador, 10 fishing schooners, six of which were British, are missing since the gale of August 23rd and following days. The number of men aboard each schooner was not less than 12. Several large vessels went ashore en Dog Island, near St. Pierre, on August 26th, and in many cases became total wrecks, the loss of life being very great. The captain of the schooner Ethel, the mate of the Ruby, two seamen of the Joseph Amaclie, and three seamen of the Acadiene, were swept off their respective vessels and lost during the hurricane along the north- west coast of America. The British trading schooner Niagara was lost with all hands, about 10 in number, on Lake Superior on the 7th inst., during a hurricane which caused great loss to shipping.

DEATH OF A BOY FROM HYDROPHOBIA IN LIVERPOOL. ---Septimus Bevan, about nine years of age, whose parents reside at 43, Farnworth-street, Liverpool, died from hydrophobia at the Royal Infirmary on Saturday morn- ing. On the 30th July last the boy was going up an entry leading to the back door of his father's house, when he noticed that he was being followed by a dog. Just before be reached the door the animal made a spring at him, and bit him in the hand, the teeth meeting. He got into the yard, and as he was shutting the door the dog made another spring at him.' It found its way after this to the Fairfield Cricket Ground, where it bit a little girl and Mrs. Atkinson during an attempt the latter made to kill it, seeing that it was mad. Lath on Thursday night Bevan showed signs of hydrophobia, and displayed a particular aversion to water and milk, and had a nasty taste in his mouth. On Friday he became worse, and suffered from convulsive fits. Be had to be restrained by force from doing injury to himself. Within ten minutes of his death the boy is reported to have been perfectly sane. Dr. Jones, house physician, has had the care of the boy since his admission to the Infirmary, Mrs. Atkinson, who has been under the treatment of M. Pasteur, it may be said, tas now returned from Paris, but is still in weak health. !There is, however, every, reason for believing that the heroic woman is on the fair way to recovery.

DESTRUCTIVE B 0; I. LOGI ON ON; A MAIL STEAMER. - GHASTLY. SCENE.—NINE KILLED. A terrible explosion, accompanied by serious loss of life, occurred on Monday afternoon, on board the : Royal Mail Company's steamer Elbe. The vessel is of 3,063 tons gross burden, and was built by Messrs. Elder and Co., at Glasgow, in 1870. A few months ago she was placed, for the purpose of having her compound engines converted to the new principle known as the triple. ; expansion, in the hands of Messrs. Oswald, Mordaunt, and Co.,proprietors ef the Southampton Shipbuilding Works, at ' Woolston. The work was completed some time Last month, and the vessel underwent a preliminaty trial at the measured mile in Stokes Bay. Some trifling defect manifested itself, which, although not actually affecting the utility of the engines, was, in the opinion of the com- pany's officials and others, of sufficient importance to necessitate a further trial. This was fixed to take place on Monday, and the Elbe left the dock on the early tide, about nine a.m. She was under the com- mand of Captain John Brander, who was chief officer of the Re.yal Mail Company's steamship Boyne, when that vessel was wrecked in the Bay of Biscay about ten years ago. There were aLso on board, Captain Bevis, the Royal Mail Company's superintendent; Mr. Bowers, the company's superintending engineer: Mr. Oswald and Mr. Mordaunt, the contractors for the new engines; Mr. Arthur, the company's assistant superintendent engineer; Mr. Thompson, the company's inspector of machinery; and many other gentlemen. The vessel pro- ceeded to Stokes Bay about noon, and two or three rains were made at the measured mile, with, it is understood, most satisfactory results, the engines proving themselves to be all it was hoped they Would be. Shortly after three o'clock. when the vessel was a little to the westward of the bay, those on deck heard a sharp crack below, of which, for the moment, but little was thought. It soon became apparent, however, that some- thing serious had really happened, for from the stoke-hole there issued a rush of steam so dense that no one, could . attempt to enter for more than an hour, although it was known that several men—among them Mr. Thompson and Mr. Ewing. the second engineer— were down below. When at last an entry was made by Dr. Aubim who was attached to the vessel for the day, and others, a fearful sight presented itself. The dead bodies of nine men, including those of Mr. Thompson and Mr. Ewing, lay scattered in various pits of the stoke-hole, terribly disfigured by the scalding steam. The ' first care was, of course, to discover whether any in the engine room or stoke-hole had escaped, and happily it proved that no other of the engineers had been injured althotigh Henry Flux; the engineers' storekeeper, who rushed out of the stoke-hole by a ladder, was so much injured by the scalding vapour that his hurts are likely to prove fatal. It appeared that the steam- pipe conducting the steam from the boilers to the en- gines had burst and caused the total disablement of the vessel. Signals were made for assistance, and the Government tug Malta went from Cowes Harbour. The poor fellow Flux was placed on board, and conveyed with all speed' to Southampton, and placed in the Royal South Hants Infirmary. Immediately upon the disaster becoming known, the steamtug Sovereign steamed down to the Elbe, and the bodies of the nine unfortunate vic- tims, wrapped in blankets and covered with sail-cloth, were placed on board. The Sovereign immediately re- turned with her ghastly freight, which she landed at the dock wharf shortly before eleven o'clock at night. The Elbe remains in Osborne Bay. The following is a list of the dead:— William Thompson, 21, chief engineer, married, One son. Walter Geo. Ewing, 41, second engineer, married, three children. Alfred Thorn, le, boiler maker, married, no children. Win. Godber, engineer at Messrs. Oswald's. Thos. Rogers, 34, fireman at Messrs. Oswald's, married, four children. George Roberts, 45, fireman to the Royal Mail Company, married, no children. Chas. Hayes, 24, fireman to the Royal Mail Company, married, no children. - Fred. H. Faustone, 22. coal trimmer, single. Geo. Paisley, 19, coal trimmer, single.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Mr. Pickersgill, M.P., and the other members of the English Home Rule deputation left Limerick on Monday for Tralee. They were cheered on departing. On Monday, the Granny Bridge National School, be- tween Kildysart and Kilrush, was burnt to the ground. It is alleged that there is ill-feeling against the teacher in the locality. The Freeman's Journal suggests that Mr. Brunner's proffered thousand should be declined. It does honour to the donor, and Irishmen will appreciate his goodness, but ,they are not mendicants. They crave no favours. They only ask Englishmen to assist them to obtain Home Rule. Claiming to be a nation, they cannot accept elee- mosynary assistance save in the presence ot famine. Just before commencement of mass, on Sunday, at Anglesborough, about four miles from Mitchelstown, on the arrival of the police from Glenacurrane to take their usual seats in the gallery, the whole of the people in the churcn left their seats and deserted the place. At Gall. batty, about five miles from Mitchelstown, the National School, which is kept by the wife of a constable, has been boycotted, and is stated to be closed. Ten men were charged under the Crimes Act at Bal. linasloe, on Saturday, with having obstructed the police in the discharge of their duty. They were each senteribed to two months' imprisonment. An appeal was entered. ./kt the Cork Police-court, on Saturday, John Barry was sentenced to a month's imprisonment for threatening Mr. Gardiner. R.M., on the occasion of Mr. O'Brien's arrest, when a crowd threw stones at the military and police. Mr. S. J'. Burke, a tenant of Lord Clanricarde's, at Clondegeff, was very cleverly evicted by the sub-Sheriff on Saturday. The building had been barricaded for some time, and twenty men had been told off to defend it when the Sheriff approached, but the Sheriff and his party came up the Shannon on yachts, and landing at six o'clock in the morning entirely surprised Mr. Burke, the eviction being completed in a few minutes. People came running in from all quarters directly afterwards, when horns sounded and the chapel bell was rung, but they were too late to affect the result. At eight o'clock 3,000 people had gathered. Mr. Henry Whiting, of Lavender-hill, Wandsworth, I.ondon, has forwarded to Capt. Francis Welch, resident magistrate, a cheque for £25. to distribute between the widow of the murdered Head-constable Whelehau and the constables engaged in the-fatal affray at the house of the man Sexton in County Clare. He also stated that if it is proposed to place the bead constable's children in an orphanage he will willingly help. Captain Welch, replying to Mr. Whiting, says it is proposed that the constabulary shall start a fund of their own. It has been asserted that the Clare authorities most providen- tially obtained information which enabled the police to save the lives of Mr. Sexton, his mother, and servant, who, beynd all doubt, were doomed to death had not the police been there to intercept the assassins. Poor Whelehan was specially despatched from Ennis to ensure the successful issue of the precautions taken for Sexton's protection. • MR. DILLON'S INTENTIONS AND VIEWS.

A correspondent in Dublin had an interview on Sunday with Mr. John Dillon, M.P., who stated that he would attend the National League Convention in Limerick on Tuesday and the Mitehelstown inquiry on Wednesday, and would 'also call on Mr. O'Brien in gaol at Cork. Mr. Dillon observed that the outlook for the autumn and winter was gloomy: It seemed to him that Mr. Bailout had made up his mind to get all the Nationalist leaders in the clutches of the law, and if the Government per- sisted in their measures of coercion it must inevitably lead to trouble. They seemed determined, added Mr. Dillon, to force an outburst of crime. The presence of the Chief Secretary in Dublin last week was significant, and to his mind portended coming trouble. If Mr. O'Bcien, after his trial, were treated as ;t, common felon there would be violent indignation. not only throughout Ireland, but in America. After referring to the recent landlords' convention hi Dublin, Mr. Dillon said that the resident magistrates as a body were grossly incom- petent; and the Irish constabulary, although a splendid body of men, were the political agents of an unpopular Government and in a constant state of hostility to the people.
THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. SUPPRESSION OF 200 BRANCHES..

The Dublin Evening lel .graph states that at the Privy Council meeting in Dublin Castle, on Tuesday, the Go- vernment decided to issue orders prohibiting the National League absolutely in the entire county 01 Clare, thereby suppressing 65 branches, and prohibiting the League in certain districts in the counties of Cork, Galviay, and Kerry. The London correspondent, from whom the news emanates, states that Long,hrea, county Galway, forming a part of the Marquis of Clanricarde's estate, and Mitchelstown, Croont, and Kanturk, county Cork, will be included in the specified districts, thus prohibiting 200 branches cf the League. Tuesday's Dublin Gazette contains the following.—

44 We, the Lord Lieutenant-General and General. Governor of Ireland, by and ,vith t lie advice of the Privy Council in Ireland, and by virtue of the Criininal Law and Procedure (Ireland) Act. 1887. and of every power and authority in this behalf, do hereby, by this our Order. prohibit and suppress, within the county of Clare, the association named and described in our special proels- rrtstion, dated 19tb August, 1887, as the Irish National League.--Given at the Council Chamber, Dublin Castle, 17th September, 1887, EDWARD Saxx-‘VEImAit, General. AstagooßSll4 C.; ARTHUR JANIRS EALMUR, RRVRT BRUNS. J. G. Gissori, REDyEas _Er.r.LER." -

The Gazette also contains similar announcements coti. cerning the National League in the barony of Leitrim. go. Galway; the barony or Loughrea, co. Galway ; the barony of Corkaguiny, co. Kerry; the barony of Condone and Clangibbon, co. Cork-; the barony of Dunhallow, Cork; the barony of West Muskerry, co. Cork; the Barony of ghelbourne, Co. Wexford.

div.head: M ITCH E LSTOWN RIOTS.
div.p: THE M ITCH E LSTOWN RIOTS.

At the MitcheltJwo inquest, on Monday, Sergeant Kir- wan's evidence WAIS continued. Hassid that after firing from the door of the barracks be went upstairs and tired two rounds of buckshot and ens of ball. He also stated that Sergeant Ryder aud Constable Gavin fired. „Inspector Irwin gave the order to protect the barracks, but not to tire nn. less stones were thrown. One stone broke a window. Gavin said that Irwin told him to fire at a man who was throwing stones.

On Tuesday the inquest was continued, when ienportant evidence was given by Miss Amy Mender, of Wolverhamp- ton, an eye-witness of the affray, and others. During the cross-examination of one witness, considerable heat was die. played by Mr. Harrington and also by the witness, and the inquest was adjourned, as the coroner said, to allow the parties to cool down. On Wednesday Mr. John Dillon, M.P., was examined at the Mitchelstown inquiry. After describing the incursion of the constabulary into the crowd, he said that when be taw the police pursued by the people be was afraid that trouble might result, and he walked rapidly towards the barrack, calling on the people not to follow, and asking one Or two priests to stop at the corner of the square and keep the people back. He found the barrack door I shut, and no policemen in sight and no crowd outside. There was nu stotie-throwing that he saw. When himself and the priest were admitted into the bar- rack, witut ss told the officer in command that their only desire was to keep the peace and avoid bloodshed, and that Übe would promise te keep his men in barrack for a little time they would undertake to clear the town. The officer replied, "No, no; I must form my men in the streets," and would not listen to anything more, and some of his men tried to push witness out a the barrack. Shortly afterwards the first shot he heard was fired. Mr. Dillon next described the brutal conduct of the police towards men they subse- ‘qaently dragged into the barrack. Firing was then g.ing on, and as soon as witnesa could again catch the officer in command, the county inspector, he said, " For God's sake stop this, and give a chance to disperse the people;" but the officer refused to accede to his request. A young officer suggested that "Mr. Dillon should have a chance," and witness was let out of the barrack. He thn saw no one near, and met nobody till he reached the square, when he heard of the slaughter. While in the barrack he heard no stones thrown at Hee building or any attempt to break the door. Witness had never before seen a tody of police attempt to bring a Government reporter through a crowd in the same way as was adopted on this occasion. He had al- ways offered a seat to a Government reporter when asked for it, but this time no such application was made. The inquiry stands adjourned to Tuesday next. Mr. Gladstone, writing to a Glasgow correspondent, says he appreciates the grave acts of the police against the people at Mitchelstown, asct the adoption and approval of them without waiting the result of the inquiry by Her Majesty's Government, and he trusts that even at this season of the year the people will not be slow to indicate condemnation of that indecent approval.

div.head: CU RRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CU RRENT POLITICS.

Earl Kimberley, speaking at a meeting at Chippenham on Saturday, said it had been made clear that the _Government's policy was to repress free political dis- cussion. He urged them to follow the example of Lord Spencer, who, administering Ireland in a time of great anxiety, steadily refused to suppress meetings until he was convinced that those assemblies would lead to a breach of the peace. The Duke of Devonshire, replying to a correspondent who drew his Grace's attention to a statement made in the newspapers that, notwithstanding Lord Hartingtones ' attitude on the Home Rule question, the Duke was a strong supporter of Mr. Gladstone's scheme, writes from Holker Hall :—" There is not the slightest foundation for the report that I are an advocate of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule policy. On the contrary, lam strongly opposed to it." At a meeting of the Stratford (London) Liberal and Radical Club, on Saturday, a resolution was adopted protesting against the infringement of the right of pub- lic meeting and the police assassinations in Ireland. Mr. Labouchere, M.P., wrote saying that the aim of the Government was to put down all constitutional rights in Ireland: The people at Mitchelstown met for a per- fectlyiegal object, and be regretted that they were not armed, and were consequently unable to teach these dis- orderly ruffians that law-abiding citizens could not be bludgeoned and shot with impunity. Spe.akin gat the! luncheon, on Saturday, at Glossop Agri- cultural Secietv's show, Major Sidebottom, M.P., said he thought there were several ways in which relief might be afforded to agriculturists in their present distress. The rates and taxes levied on farmers and agricultural land were in his epiniop too high. Scme mitieation of their burdens would be found in the grant of £250,00Ce a year for the maintenance of main roads which Perlis- tnent had agreed to in the pa.st session. In the course of the next session he hoped something would be done to remove the existing inequalities in railway rates. It seemed a monstrous injustice that foreign producers should be allowed to send their goods over English lines of railway at lower rates than the home producer. Lord Hampden presided, on Saturday afternoon last, at the Glynde harvest home, and spoke on the question of allotments. He said undoubtedly they were of great advantage to the working classes. He had done all he could to provide allotments for those in his own employ, but he coneidered the pos- session of a good garden of the first importance, especially if tie allotments were situated a long distance from the workmen's dwellings'. lie hoped the measure just passed in Parliament would result in providing spaces of ground for ecenpet ion by the working classes where they were not now obtalnaide. One of the inci- dents of the year at Glynde had been the establishment of his new business as a dairy farmer. In feet, be might describe himself as a dairyman in search of profit. At present the experiment had not been tried long enough to ascertain results on which to calculate its measure of success; but it gave premise of a good result, which he hoped to report later on. In the session of close upon eight months, It hich has jest expired, the House of ,Commons had before it no less than 319 public bills, of which 249 were introduced by private members, and 70 by the Government. Or the private members measnres, writes the Manchester Coorier London Correspondent, the large majority dis- appeared before the second reeding, and only 1.9 passed into law. Sir John Lubbock passed to bills, and among the other private intenhers olio have contributed to the Statute Book this year are Mr. 11. Vincent, Dr. Cameron, Sir E. Bite:beck. Mr. C. Achim!, Mr. Felton, Mr. Blake, Mr. Haldane, Sir A. Rollie Mr. Tomlinson, and Mr. 13raillangli. Thent were time bills introduced relating to the tenure of 1.41-1. 10 relating to the liquor - traffic, and six leankraptcy.bills. Altogether 77 public bills received the Royal .assent. Of private bills 222 were introduced during the session, of which 159 became law. including three divorce bills, and there were also 37 provisional orders hills passed,-

PROPOSED TESTIMONIAL TO TIIE MAYOR AND MAYORESS OF WARRINGTON. On Monday, at noon, a meeting which had been convened by circular was held in the Mayor's Par- lour at the Town Hall, for the purpose of consider- ing what "fitting recognition should be made of the happy and harmonious manner in which the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington fulfil the duties of their position." The circular was sigfted by Alderman Holmes, Alderman Davies, Mr. Robert Davies, Alderman J. Crosfield. Alderman turgess, Alderman Chandley, Mr. John Fairclough, and Mr. F. Monks. In addition to these gentlemen, there were also present—the Rev. E. C. E. Carlton, Rev. S.W ilkinson, Rey. J. A. Drummond, Dr. C.White, Dr. Starkie Smith, Dr. Fox, Alderman Sutton, Council- lors Francomb, Jolley, Dakin, Fleming, Hutchinsm, Tinsley, Wright; Messrs. Robert Pierpoint, J.P., W. •D. Jeans, W. Owen, Thomas' Robinson, R. Dobson, ' W. Dutton, Alfred Woods, F. W. Monks, J. Hepherd, C. Myer, &c.—Alderman Hoi.mßs was elected to preside, and he briefly referred to the objects of the gathering. Letters of apology for non-attend- ance were received from Mr. J. G. McMinnies, Mr. J. Charlton Parr, Mr. J. F. Greenall, Mr. W. Sharp, Mr. T. Morris, the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, and the Rev. W. Quekett. Mr. McMinnies wrote that he should "be glied to join in any movement which may be set on foot to express the appreciation which our esteemed Mayor and Mayoress have so well and so amply earned," and the other letters were written of a similar tenour.—Alderman CROSIFIELD then proposed, Mr. R. Davres seconded the resolution, and it was agreed tounanimously— "That a luncheon be given to the Mayor and Mayoress, and that a suitable present be given to the Mayoress, which she shall have the opportu- nity of selecting."—Alderntan CILOSFIELD also pro- posed—" That a subscription be entered into to carry out the foregoing resolution, and that the amount of subscription do not exceed two guineas." —Alderman DAvifis seconded the resolution, and it was agreed to.—The following gentlemen were ap- pointed as a committee to carry out the above reso- lutions :—Alderman C. J. Holmes, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. W. D. Jeans, Mr. F. Monks, Mr. Robert Pier- point, Alderman Crosfleld, Alderman Davies, Alder- manand Councillor-Jolley. THE people of the United States have been -celebrating the hundredth birthday of their Constitution on a great scale and with great 'enthusiasm. The immortal document which 'forms the basis of the Government of the United States, and which has stood so well the test of time, was signed by the ConVen- Von, in Independence Hall, on September 17th, 1787. On Saturday last, September etch, 1887, President CLEVELAND delivered a centennial address to some thousands of 'citizens who had met at Philadelphia, in In- dependence Square. Patriotic songs were sung by two thousand children, and the Speeches were preceded by prayer and the Singing of an appropriate hymn. The Ameri- cans are proud of their Constitution, and they have reason to be proud. It was drawn up thoughtfully by thoughtful men who had t struggled for the freedom of the land they loved. Knowing something of the tyranny of kings, they proceeded on the assumption that that government would be wisest and best which had its origin in the people themselves. It was an experi- Ment of great moment a hundred years ago: to-day it can no longer be regarded as an experiment; it is in the nature 'Of a fact which has been demonstrated in a 'thousand ways. America owes much to heri harneasurable natural resources ; bat she I 'owes much, too, to the Constitution which I Preached and put into practice the doctrine Of "Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity." It is true that so long as slavery existed it was a foul blot upon the Constitution; but slavery was a legacy—a hateful legacy—of the old world; I fld was not to be got rid of by a Declaration I °f Independence. It remained for well nigh! three.quarters of a century to mock and tor- I lure the bulk of the liberty-loving people of America, until one day the hydra-headed Izonster trampled the national flag in the mire, tiol from that day its fate was sealed. It was I a terrible struggle—that struggle with the lave-holding S )uth, but the majority of the Ustion were inspired by a love of country and , a hatred of slavery ; and thousands upon thousands of America's best ard bravest sons aeroically yielded up their lives for their coun- try and their kind. The rebellion was crushed, and, better still, the stain of slavery was wiped from the face of the land. Civil War was an awful price to pay for this freedom; but. .•,s there was no alternative, it was paid wil- -4.11g1y ; and the world owes it to the valiant tikht-minded men who now inherit the united States that a State founded upon slavery as a "divine institution " did not !ear its head high in air and mock humanity °Y its unspeakable crimes. The Constitution 1787 survived the enormous strain which as put upon it by the great war; and it is ot in the nature of things that it will ever tested in a similar way. Government in he United States is not perfect in 1887 ; but .trhat is because human nature is not perfect. iS at least free from the meddling and mud- Luing of kings, lords, and state-paid priests. 41.„01rie Rule operates everywhere in the ‘Juited States, and it is by and under this taode of government that our Amorican cousins have made greater progress ma- terially, socially, and intellectually than any other natinn either of this period or'any other 12et in the world's history. They have no State church; but churches rise without State aid as they have never risen in this 1:1111.1try. Instead of teaching disputable heology, the States teach the indisputable 4' three R's," and that, too, in free schools jay.hich are beloved of the people from the lghest to the lowest. They are, as they ‘!Ornetimes boastingly speak of themselves, a ,at people ;" and, as they are for the part bone of our bone and flesh of our , we in this country can with all sincerity ce with them in their Centennial, and that the shadow of their greatness may grow less.

' The Ship Canal Company has already been in difficulties ; but, start not, it was nothing very serious; merely a hauling up at the Liverpool Police Court, on Wednesday, and a fine of los. and costs for making too much smoke on their ve3sel the Queen of the Mer- sey. It is like Liverpool—this petty interfer- ence; but let us wait till " the sweet by and by;" Liverpool may be made to smoke yet.

Apuddler named Alfred Stokes was brought before the Warrington mag.istrates, on Wed- nesday, for deserting his wife and refusing to maintain her. They were married on Jubilee Monday; but have lived together on such miserable terms that they would have done well to take " Punch's " advice to those about to marry—" don't ; " or at any rate to have postponed the event until next Jubilee Monday.

So the Irish Land League is to be sup- pressed. Drive discontent under the surface, and it does not exist, according to the Tory doctrine. Make a wilderness, and call it peace. But does anybody think that where a Forster failed a Balfour will succeed ? Besides, then Ireland stood alone; now she has Wales and Scotland, and half of England with her. Let Irishmen show a little more patience, and they will beat Balfour and all his works.

Curious sport—setting fire to and burning down a grand stand and refreshment-room. Yet this is what was done, at Lillie Bridge Grounds, near London, on Monday, and all because a race which was counted on did not come off. And this is the nineteenth century, and London is the centre of civilisa- tion. Scratch a racing rough, and you find a savage that would disgrace a Hottentot. If such a thing had happened in Ireland, the Coercionists would have been ready to say : " I told you so." Wnat will they say now?

At the adjourned Brewster Sessions, at Warrington, on Tuesday, the Magistrates I in- timated to Mr. Gittens, of the Swan Inn, 11 that, if there was any breach of the law dur- ing the next twelve months the license would 1 for the future be withheld. This is an ad- -1 mirable regulation; it puts the publican on his good behaviour. But why not make the same rule apply all round ? It would be no loss to the community if licenses were withdrawn from all disorderly houses.

The Conservative agent has been made to pay "smart money" very freely in conse- quence of the number of his bad objections. He had to pay £l7 99. 6d. as against £3 jos. paid by the •Liberal agent. It would seem that on Monday he had emptied the coffers of the Conservative party, for he "ran out" when called upon to pay two guineas tor ex- penses. However, at the suggestion of the Revising Barrister, the Liberal agent came to his rescue and tent him a guinea. A Liberal agent should, of course, be liberal.

By way of repayment, Mr. Hampson has published a return in which he makes out a gain on the revision of gz. This is a pretty little fiction. The value of the return may be judged when it is stated that the Conservative agent takes credit for Liberal lodgers "not claimed for this year." Why did he not add to his list all Liberal elec- tors who have been left off the list through deaths, removals, &c.? When he goes in for moonshine, he might as well turn on the full moon.

The presentation of an address to Mr. Mc- Minnies, on Thursday evening, in commem- oration nf his seventieth birthday, was made in feeling terms by air. John Crosfield, who has been in harness for a generation with the leader of the Liberal party in Warrington. Mr. McMinmes responded in a speech which young politicians would do well to study and lay to heart. He preaches what he has prac- tised; he has won golden opinions from all sorts of men; and everyone wishes that he may continue to enjoy that which should accompany old age, As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends.

The failure of the Warwick Bank has brought distress upon an unusually large number of people who made use of it as a means of investment. These people had every confidence in its soundness on account of its age. The failure enforces an old moral; those who want security as strong as the nation must go to the nation itself—that is to the Post Office Savings Bank. Even ordinary Savings Banks, with what is called Government security, are not as strong by comparison.

The horrors of the Doncaster railway disas- ter are of a kind to " make each particular hair to stand on end." There is need for the most searching investigation. It came out at the Government inquiry, on Monday, that the block system is always suspended on the St. Leger and Cup days; that is to say, people travel on these occasions with the sword of Damocles over their heads. It would be interesting to ascertain whether it is the custom throughout the country to dis- pense with the block system during Whitsun- tide and other excursions. The public have a right to know what is the real risk they run when they enter a railway carriage.

It seems that the member for the Newton Division has been in the hands of brigands, and effected his release without paying a ransom by passing himself off as a servant. The question is sometimes debated in Mutual Improvement Classes whether, under any cir- cumstances, a lie is justifiable. Mr. T. W. Legh gives an answer in the affirmative. But then he is not a moralist—he is an M.P. And besides he has been in the diplomatic service; and amongst diplomatists an assertion which is not true is not a lie ; it is merely a dip- lomatic statement. However, Mr. Legh has escaped, and we congratulate him on his freedom. •

CABINET MAKING FOR AIIATEITUS.—A number, of interesting articles on this subject are at present appearing in the monthly issues of "Amateur Work," from the pen of Mr. David Adamson, of the eminent firm of Urquhart and Adamson, house fur- nishers, Bold-street, Liverpool. The subject consi- dered in the current issue is" An overmantel for amateurs; how to make it and finish it." An ele- gant substitute for the customary mirrors in this piece of furniture is found. in elegantly-designed carved panels of wood; obviating the objection of some authorities that too great a use of mirrors destroys on account of the glitter, the feeling of repose which is an end sought in their schemes of decoration. The directions given throughout the text are eminently practical and exhaustive, numer- ous working and other drawings accompanying the descriptions. With the valuable aid here offered the amateur of any pretensions to the skilful use of tools need never be at the loss as to the modus operandi of accomplishing good and lasting work in house decoration and furnishing. Brunner, the successful candidate, amouuted to £1,465 54 ; while those of Lord Henry Grosvenor totalled £1,401 17s sd. HALTON PARISI( CHURCH.—Special services in corinec- lion with the Sunday schools were held on Sunday. The Rev. J. Eaves, vicar of Feirtield, Buxton, occupied the pulpit both morning and evening, and the services were full choral. The sum of £3 17s 34 realised by the c Alections will be devoted to the fund for purchasing Bibles and prayer and hymn books. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT FARNWORTIL—This festival was continued at Farnworth Parish Church on Sunday. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, vicar of Holy Trinity, Warrington, preached in the morning, and in the evening the Rev. J. E. Lawton, the curate at Farnworth, occupied the pulpit. The choir rendered several anthems, the solos being sung by Miss Fagg, and Mr. J. R. Lea. The collections were in aid of the Curates' Fund. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES —The annual harvest thanksgiving ser- vices were held in Milton Congregational Church on Sun- day. The building had been appropriately decorated, and presented a charming appearance. The Rev. Thomas Cole, of Garston, preached to fair congregations. The choir, con- ducted by Mr. J. Poole, rendered specially selected hymns and anthems in good style. OPEN.AIR CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—MiII Brow Military Band on Wednesday evening performed tde following pro. gramme of music in Devonshire-rquare :—March, "Drift- ing with the tide ; " lancers, "Fun and frolic"; vela, "Bitter sweet" ; grand selection, "I Puritani " (with solos foe principal performer) ; chorus, "To Thee, 0 Lord polka," Merrie bells"; "God save the Queen." The last concert will take place on Wednesday evening, September 28th,, in Devonshire-square, at 730. THE SALVATION ARMY AT RUNCORN.—The members of this branth of the Salvation Army, on Sunday, held special services of thanksgiving for the bounteous harvest. The citadel WAS skilfully decorated with cereals, fruits, and flags sod mottoes. Two portraits of General Booth occupied prominent positions. Major Rees. chief officer of the Man- chester Division, conducted the services, and the building was crowded. On Monday morning an officers' meeting was held, and in the afternoon a holiness meeting took place, about 30 officers being present. On Monday evening the harvest festival was cvntinued, and Deere was a crowded audience. Winterbottom, g-ocer, of Moss Bank, was seriously injured on Tuesday. When returning from school at noon that day, a number of Winterbottoin'e com- panions jumped across a ditela. Winterbottom, iu attempting the feat, fell into the ditch head fore:nost, and was fright- fully cut on the face and head by the various hard sub- stances that were lying atout. His head was cut open from the forehead to the ear, the wound being about 7in. in length, about 3in. wide, and very deep. Dr. Saul, assistant to Dr. O'Neil, was passing at the time and gave the boy every attention. Me is not yet out of danger. CHOIR TREAT A? RUNCOEN.—The choir of St. Michaels and All Angels Church had their annual treat on Saturday last. Accompanied by Mr. Sumrnerfield, the churchwarden, the party, numbering 25, proceeded to Chestsr by the 12.46 train, and immediately on arriving at the city a boat was chartered for Eccleston Ferry. The afternoon was pleasantly spent in exploring the beauties and wonders of the palatial mansion of the Duke of Westminster. Upon returning to Chester the party act down to an excellent tea ! at the Hop Pole Hotel. The vicar and churchwardens were heartily thanked for their kindness on the proposition of Mr C. rawnell, seconded by Mr. J. Good well. Mr. G. Summer. field responded. THE TALE or THE Tower.— Howell's Golden Herb SERIOUS TRAP ACC:JOHN? AT WIDNES.—A serious acci- dent occurred in Victoria-road about eight o'clock on Fri- day evening last week. Two daughters of Mrs Ashley, innkeeper and milk dealer, Appleton, were driving past the Alexandra Hotel, when suddenly the fore legs of the horse sunk into the ground up to the knees, with the result that the trap was upset and the occupants were thrown violently out. Startled by its strange pesition the horse commenced to kick violently with its hind legs, and besides severely injuring itself smashed the trap. , The animal WAS eventually extricated and an, examination showed that the road, in which the new m lin sewer has been recently laid, had been rendered quite soft with the heavy rains of the previous week, and had sunk below the usual level. The occupants of the trap were bruised and shaken, and had to be assisted home. SAD DEATH OF & BOY AT WIDNES.--OR Monday, at the West Bank Hotel, Widnes, Mr. W. T.. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Thomas Roscoe, 13 years of age, son of Thomas, Roscoe, gas stoker, of 17 Church-street. The boy had been missing since the Bth inst ; and his dead body was found floating in the Widnes and St. Helens Canal on Saturday last by a Waterman named Hickson. It appeared that OD the evening of the day mentioned a youth named Whitehead, whose parents live in Oakland-street, saw the deceased on the side of the canal near Messrs Gossage's works. He was then engaged" fish- ing with two tins." Whitehead asked him to come home, but he refused, and a few days later, hearing of the boy's disappearance, Whitehead informed Sergeant Robinson of the incident. The canal was dragged, but without result, and the boy's body was recovered as stated. A verdict of "Found deed" was returned. RUNCORN BOWLING Cum.—The members of the Runcorn Bowling Club, which has its head quarters at the South Bank Hotel, brought a most enjoyable season to a conclu- sion on Thursday by a pleasant reunion. In the afternoon 37 members engaged in a friendly main at bowls, Mr. Thos. Cooper having handicapped each competitor on his merits. The result was that the first prize of 10s Was won by C Faulkner, and the second of Os by S Thompson. S Worrell and .1 Raynor each secured 4s, while a prize of 2s was awarded to J Laverock, J Bebbington, and Jolly. Seven other members each received a shilling. Subs•quently the members adjourned to the South Bank Hotel, where they partook of a sumptuous repast prepared by Mrs Jones. Mr Thomas Cooper presided, and the vice-chair was occupied by Mr J Coxhill. After the table had been dlearert the cut. ternary toasts were prepared and duly honoured, and a con- vivial evening was spent. songs and recitations being given amongst others by Messrs George Turley, J D Widders, H Johnson, P Smith, and J Ravenscroft, who accompanied. CONCERT AT WIDNES —With the object of augmenting the funds of the Simms Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel, a concert was held in the Volunteer Hall on Monday, and was a decided success, both from a musical and a financial point of view. The large building was comfortably filled throughout. Mr Eustace Carey, who presided, opened the proceedings with a brief speech, in which he observed that that excellent audience testified that the Widnes people still maintained their character for kind heartedness and liberal- ity of sentiment. Widnes men were always ready to help people who were earnest in their endeavour to do good, no matter to what denomination they belonged. A most attrac- tive programme was presented, the vocalists being as fol- lows :—Madame Palmira Bouvini, prima donna soprano from Milan, formerly of the Italian Opera House, Nice; Miss Annie Parry, contralto, Birkenhead, winner of the first prize at the Royal National Eisteddfod; Mr. George Barton, the well-known tenor; and Mr. Edward Grime, basso, from the Crystal Palace, London. The appreciation of the audience was strongly marked, each artiste being credited with an encore. The hurecnirous element was ably contributed by Mr R D Rodgers, of Liverpool. The Liver- pool Standard Quartett Party were as popular as ever. Mr Geerge Eyton. organist of Renshaw-street Baptist Chapel, was the accompanist. Under the leadership of Mr W Jen- nett,the Soap Works Brass Band performed several pieces of music in an acceptable manner. INDIGESTION CURED by ens bex of Howell's Golden Herb Pills.—Adet. RUNCORN FREE Primo LIBRARY.—The annual meeting was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday. Present : Messrs J Simpson, W Handley, F A Lake, .1 11 Frith, G Moss, W Hankinson, T Riley, E Marwood, an 4 3 D Jones (librarian.) The first business was the election of chairman for the ensuing year.—Mr Simpson proposed that Mr W Handley, whom be described as the father of the Free Library, should succeed Mr Lake as chairman. It was his (Mr. Simpson's) opinion that the town would not have had a free library if Mr Handley' had not agitated the matter some years before the question was thoroughly taken up.— Mr F A Lake seconded the proposition, remarking that Mr Handley was thoroughly well qualified for the post of chairman. Of the three gentlemen who were instrumental in obtaining the adoption of the Free Libraries Act in Runcorn Mr Handley was the only one they lead now on the committee.—The motion was unanimously carried, and Mr. Handley took the chair. He said he should have great pleasure in fulfilling the duties, especially when he remem- bered that the proceedings of the committee had always been characterised by the greatest hartncny.—Oa the pro- position of Mr Frith, seconded by Mr. Moss, and supported by Mr Simpson and the Chairrnan,the cordial thanks of the committee were accorded to Mr Lake for his past services RS chairman.—On the proposition of Mr MOSS, seconded be' Mr Riley, the Rev A Maitland Wood, M.A., was appointed vice-chairmare—The Librarian reported that during the past month there had been 1,565 volumes issued from the lending department.

--,.- --- HARVEST FESTIVAL AT RUSCORN PARISE CHURCH On lbursday evening the annual harvest thanksgiving ser- vice WAS held in Runcorn Parish Church. Fruit, divers, and cetials bad been used in a very artistic manner to deco- rate the sacral edifice, which presented a most pretty ap- pearance. The service was full choral. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Canon Cooper, M.A., rector of Tar- Polley, and rural dean of Middiewich, who preached from the text " How much owest thou unto my Lord." The collection was in aid of the curates' fund. fleuvasT FxsTrver. AT ST. PAUL'S CHURCII,WIDNES The thanksgiving sorvic-s at St. Paul's Clureb were Con- Clltlei on Sunday. In the morning the Vicar occupied the pulpit, and the reverend gentleman also addressed the scholars in the afternoon. The preacher in the evening was the Rev. F. B. Tvrer, ICC, of St. Saviour's. Liverpool. The choir, under the leaderqhip of Mr. Raison, rendered several anthems in good style, the solos being taken by , Mr. Broughton, Mr. T. Walker, and Master C. Bale. A VIOLENT CARTER AT Surrosr.—John Hulse was aura- monecl to Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting James Fletcber..—Halse was represen- ted by his wife —lt appeared that on the 10th inst. Hulse i was unloading a cart at Sutton Bridge, and Mr. Rigby corn• plained to him of the manner in which he was doing the work. The defendant used very bad language to Mr. i Rigby, who walked away. Fletcher, who is the bridge ten- ter, remonstrated with the defendant, metro then assaulted him. The defendant was drunk at the time. These facts having been corroborated by P.S. Oldlield. the Bench ins. I posed a fine of Ll and costs for the assault, and lOs and costs for the drunkenness. StICIDE AT Wirmas.--On Thursday, John. Howard. 38 years of age, who was employed as a labourer at the Thars.s Copper Works, and lived in Appleton Village, committed suicide. About eight months ago Howard's wife died, and since then he has been much addicted to drinking. At 10, o'clock on Wednesday night he went to bed as usual, and at five o'clock next morning his sister heard him walking about downstairs. Thinking he was sick, she took no fur- ther steps in the matter, but upon descending into the kit- , chen at eight °clock she found her brother hanging. by the j neck to a rope which was attached to a beam. An alarm , was given, and a neighbour named Joseph Heyes cut the rope. Life was, however, entirely extinct. THEFT AT Btervote Wksvitte—Before Mr. John Brundrit , and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Jemes Morton, a boatman, of Northwich, was , charged with stealing a pair of trousers, the property of Joseph Hinde, of Sutton Weaver. On the 21st inst. the , trousers were washed and placed upon a hedge to dry. They were left there at night, and next morning were not to be foiled. Mrs Hinds complained of her loss to some boatman, and threatened to. inform the police. The prisoner hearing , of this, went to a stable and brought forth the trousers, which he replaced upon the hedge. He was apprehended by P.S. Oldfield,. and stated that his intention was to i take care of the troueers. He was sentenced to seven days' , hard labour. ALLEGED GAMBLING. AT' Fat/NCAIN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday,. William Lovell, aged 14, and Michael Thomas Dowell, aged 13i were summoned for playing at pitch and toss nearthe railway station on the Bth inst.— P.C. 141 deposed to seeing the defendants toss coins at the Holloway. Upon seeing the officer the boys decamped, I but were chased, and one being captured gave a wrong name and address. The station master had constantly I complained of the practice, and the constable had been specially instructed to watch for gamblers —The defendants I pleaded that they were playing with buttons for fun.-The magistrates consideled the case proved, but as this was the first appearance of the defendantikthev were dismissed with a caution. Tne genet, wished it to become known that ' future offenders would be severely punished. FAMILY DESERTION AT RUNONIN.—At Runcora Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. J. Brandrit and Captain liazlehurst, a labourer, named John Bowman, was charged with deserting his family, who bad in consequence become chargeable to the common fund of the Runcorn Union. Mr. W. H. Linaker prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians. It ' appeared that about 18 months ago the prisoner's wife sepa- rated from him owing to his misconduct, and she obtained a situation as a servant in Liverpool. On two occasions Mr. Ward, the relieving officer, had defendant's two children admitted as inmates to the woikhouse, but. be had in each instance quickly discharged himself, and sometime ago he departed from the town. He left his children totally no- provided for, but a woman named Mrs Williams took care of them for a time, but the expense being too great for her limited resources they were sent to the workhouse. The re- lieving officer had ascertained that the prisoner could have employment anytime he liked to askat Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele, but he was an idle, worthless fellow. Mr. Line. tar said this was a very bad case, and asked the Bench to make au example of him. There were many cases of a similar nature in the union. The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. CRUELTY TO A. HORSE AT WU:Mew-At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday. before Mr. H. Gaekell, sem., and Mr. T. Sutton Timm's, Thomas Hawkins, greengrocer, Widnes- road, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state, and Walter Biggs, a young man, was charged with working the animal. P.S. Strickland deposed that on the afternoon of the 12ch inst. a horse attached to a spring cart, loaded lightly with ham- pers, was standing in front of Hawkins' shop. Biggs said he was in charge of the horse, and the sergeant, upon ex- amination, found the animal suffering from two wounds under the saddle, from one of whioh matter was issuing. 'there was also a wound upon each shoulder. B Ala defen- dants made a statement to the same effect—that they were quite aware the wounds were there. The horse, they alleged, had been kept up for'two or three days, but it was wanted to remove some garbage from the back premises, as "Mr. Dickson gets on to us so."—P.C. Davy corroborated.— Hawkins now denied that he was aware the horse was working —Mr. Gaskell said the Bench were of opinion that in this case, as in most cases of a similar character, the em- ployer was to blame, and Hawkins would be fined se, and costs 121. The case against Biggs was dismissed. Tint PIG-KEEPING NUISANCE AT Wternss.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, en Thursday, Robert Simeon, grocer, Char- lotte-street, was summoned at the instance of John Dickson, nuisance inspector to Widnes Local Board, for keening on his premises pigs which were in a filthy condition and a nuisance.—Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the Board, produced the new bye-laws which had been approved by the Local Government Board, and which came into force on the 9th July. By these bye-laws it was an offence to keep pigs within a distance of fifty feet of a dwelling-house, and the defendant kept pigs in the back yard of his house. On the firet September the defendant was served with a notice to remove the pigs within seven days, but he bad failed to obey the order. In conseqeence of the numerous cases of disease there had been in the township recently the Local Board had decided to do away with the keeping of pigs in back yards. , —The defendant said the premises where these pigs were , kept were not occupied as a dwelling-house, but were used ass store-room and a shop—Mr. Dickson stated that the de- fendant occupied three email shops. He lived in one building and rented the back part of another shop to a family. The pigs were not more than 20 feet from the defendant's own house.—Dr. Cooper said the pi4s were kept in a filthy con- dition, and constituted a nuisance dangerous to public health.—Upon the defendant promising to remove the pigs at once Mr. Allen withdrew the commons.

A New THEATRE FOR Waimas.—During thepsst few years there have been several attempts made to fiesta company ' for the purpose of erecting and managing a new theatre at Widnes. At last the efforts have borne fruit. A company, of which Messrs. Thomas Gerrard, Charles Sutcliffe, and William Bray are the principal shareholders, has been formed, and plans, drc., have been prepared by Mr. James Rimmer, architect and surveyor. The site of the new build- ing is in Alexandra-street, off Victoria-road, a position which is central and convenient to the several railway stations. The architectural style of the proposed building is described as Italian Gothic. The front of the building will present a very handsome appearance, being of Doulton bricks with red stone dressings, with a terracotta panel run- ning the entire width. The main entrance will be by a veran- dah supported by oast iron pillars and framework,with stained glass panels, and will be approached by five steps leading into a lobby. Ou the top stores are to be three sets of double stained glass windows, separated by four busts of famous poets. The entire length of the building is to be 115 feet, and the width 60 feet. The stage will occupy 40 feet of the length, and the roof over this portion of the structure will be raised an additional thirty feet in order that the scenes may be lifted bodily, As a precaution in times of fire there will he an iron drop curtain. The provisions for egress are to be exceedingly good. Two windows are to be placed on each side of the gallery, undereeath which are to be fixed fire escapes, which may be put through the windows or lowered into the pit. There will be other numerous outlets for the audience in else of panic. It is estimated tbat the building will seat 1,500 persons comfor- tably, and the cost is put down at £3,000. Building opera- tions have been already commenced, and the shareholders hope to have the theatre ready for performances during the winter.

Upon the case of Isabella Heath against her husband be. lag called at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. J. W. Knowles, who appeared for Mrs Heath, said she was endeavouring to compel her husband to maintain her. A fortnight ago Mr. Swift, barrister, of Liverpool, appeared for the defendant, and tie (Mr. Knowles) arranged with him that the defendant should pay his wife 7s 6d per week, and in order that that agreement could be drawn up lay Mr. P ters, acting as solicitor for the other side, the case was ad- journed. From that day until this Mr. Peters bad refused to carry out the Agreement as arranged, but wanted to make an agreement compelling the wife to accept a great deal stronger terms than was decided upon. He (Mr. Knowles) declined to make a fresh agreement. The poor woman was really in want of bread and she was willing to sign any- thing. He had told her that morning that she could sign what she liked, but by his authority and by his sanction she should sign nothing more than was agreed. She said she would sign anything for bread, and he believed she had been to Mr. Peter's office and made some terms behind his back. He should offer no evidence that day.—Mr. Peters: I should like to say a word or two. —Mr. Lewin (magistrates' clerk) : The magistrates do not wish to hear what is between yon and Mr. Knowles.—Mr. Peters : I ask that I should be allowed in all fairness and courtesy to speak against the serious charges made by my hiend.—Mr. Knowles : If he wants to talk about unprofes- eional conduct, be should have to make some charges.—Mr. Gaskell : We have nothing to do with the case further.— Mr. Peters: I wish to say that Mr. Knowles' statement is entirely untrue. Mr. Peters was about to make some fur- ther observations, when he was interrupted by Mr. Gaskell. —Mr. Peters then asked why Mr. Knowles was allowed to speak, and Mr. Gasket( replied that he thought Mr. Knowles was opening his case. It was, he said, evident that some feeling existed, and the magistrates had nothing to do with Peters : Do you dismiss the case.—Mr. Gaskell : We don't dismiss it. We have nothing before ue.—Mr. Guskell added that no doubt the reporters would take no. tics of Mr. Peters' statement —Mr. Peters : Anl I hope they will put down that your worships would vot allow me the right te reply.—The other business was then proceeded I with.

Mr. Peters requests us to state, as the Bench considered Mr, finowles's remarks too irrelevant to be replied to, that (I)The agreement was agreed to by both sides with the exception of one clause which Mr. Peters felt bound to in- sist on ler his client's protection, which clause provithd for forfeiture of the wife's allowance if she molests her husband or injures his property. (2) Mr. Knowles was incorrect in stating in court that the matter was then set- tied. The fact was that Mrs Heath called severai times during the fortnight at Mr. Peters' office, but Mr. Peters refused to listen to her, and told her to instruct her solici- tor, and when Mr. Peters went to court, on Thursday, he fully expected that Mr. Knowles would have received and have been prepared to carry out his client's instructions on the point first mentioned, instead of which Mr. Knowles acted on quite unfounded suspicions.

• RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB. What promises to be one of the most successful seasons this club has ever experienced commences to-day, when the first term meet the Rochdale Hornets at Runcorn. Last I year the club justly earned the proud title of " Champions I of Cheshire," and, besides, vanquished several of the crock I clubs of Lancashire and Yorkshire. The reputation thus I gained has enabled the enthusiastic and energetic secretary, I Mr. J. E. Langshaw, to obtain a list of fixtures second to none in the football world. Swinton, Salford, Bradford, Liverpool, Dewsbury, and other famous football organisa- dons have given return d :Les, and during the next few I months Runcorn will have an opportunity of viewing , splendid displays of skill with the " oval." Encouraged by past successes, and emboldened by the prospects for the ' future, the committee have not been idle during the summer 'months. Having regard to the convenience and comfort of the thousands (:)! spectators that will assemble, they have scent no leas a sum than .£l3O upon improving the field off Canal-street. In the first place the tortuous and dangerous entrance to the " sixpenny side" has been completely done away.with. There is now a capital approach, and whilst members and players oth be comfortably admitted through a separate entrance, the public will have to pass through a patent regiatsring turnstile. The bustle and discomfort of the old clumsy system will be obviated, and the club will benefit by the increased security. Similar alterations have also been made to the top portion of the field. The ground, too, is now completely boarded round,. and the hundreds who have ben in the habit of taking a cheap view from the outside will either have to pat their hands In their pockets or miss the sport. The two classes of spectators—the "threepenny " and the " six- penny " are now completely divided by a wooden partition. Nor has the field of play been neglected. Formerly it was somewhat narrower than the limit fixed by the Rugby rules ; it is now the full width, and while the touch line was pre- yioinsly near the spectators, it is now fully a distance of five yards away. There is thus less danger to the players, and a better view for the spectators. Many other improve- ments too numerous to particularise have been mode, and the whole of the work has beea satisfactorily carried out under contract by Messrs. T. Kirkbarn and Co. A sub- committee consisting of Messrs. W. Carroll, W. Riley, 11. Andrews, and the secretary have bad the supervision of the work. It will be gratifying to the numerous football enthnsiasts in Runcorn to learn that the composition of the first team will remain practically unaltered. In fact the only change is amongst the forwards. Hoffiand, who seldom donned his jersey last year, is given another chance, and P Riley has been drafted from the second team, so that he may have an opportunity of showing his metle. J Lewis, a hard-work- ing player, will not take his position in the team for some weeks. There is every reason to belive that the team will maintain their last season's form, even if they do not sur- pass it. Their opponents, however, are af the strongest, and they must occasionally taste the bitters of defeat, but with combination and determination a prond record may be pre- dicted. To tackle Rochdale Hornets for a commencement is no mean task, but the club as formerly will rise to the occa- sion, and with Hugh Hughes to lead, the following team will to-day make a bold bid for victory :—Woods, back ; Davies, Speakman, and Cawley, three•quarter hacks; H Hughes and Andrews, half-backs; W Wright, W Hughes, G Wainwright, J Barnes, Clarke, W Broady, W Faulkner, Reiland, and P Riley, forwards; 3 Gatley, reserve.

A WIDNES THEATRICAL MANAGER AND HIS LICENSE.

At the Widnes Petty Sessione, on Thursday, Mr W Mel- lon, proprietor and manager of the Theatre Royal, asked the • magistrates (Messrs 11 07tekell, sent, and TS Timmis) to fix a special session for the purpose of bearing his applica• tion for the renewal of the license to the theatre.—Mr Gaskell observed that he came from Liverpool to hear this ' application lest week.—Mr Mellon : My two sureties did not come—.Me Gaekell : You did not come yotpself.—Mr Mellon Because I was looking for them.—Mr Oaskell : I shall not came again. I came last week at conside,able in- cormenienee to myself, and other magistrates came. and we were silt rig here all morning. We sent the police for you, , and they found you chinking. Yee, they Mend you drink- ing, and you would not put in an am/vanes.— vlr Mellon: For the simple reason that I could Not get my suretise,i.— Mr Gaskell From what has taken place Ido not cansider you a tit inan to be entrusted with a license.—Mr Mellon : ' I have hid it ti,ve year.. I have Nothing againet me. The theatre is well conducted ; nothing at all against it during the time I have had it.—:-.uperintendent Johnson : I believe he has conducted the theatre very well. He was drunk on one or two @SC./M.)lls, but he was away from business.—Mr Gaskell : I do not think such a man ought to be entrusted with a license. We will call a special session, but! shall not come. It I (lid I should be • pposed to giving you a license. It will be better for you if I am not here.—Mr Mellon.tben left the witness box, where he had bean stand- ing.

MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AND,.THR. MITCRELSTOWN
AFFRAI%

A meeting called by the North-East Manchester Liberal Association to protest against the suppression of freedom in Ireland," was held on Tuesday ereeing. at the New Is- lington Elan, Ancoats. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. H. Holland. Mr. Brunner, M.P., said he thought he was- addressing a "square-headed lot," and, he bad, therefore, confidence in submitting to them the following resolution That we claim for onr Irish fellow couratrvmen the stme right of free speech and personal liberty which we would defend at all costs for ourselves ; to resist by all the means in our power the policy of tyranny and bloodshed upon which the Government has embarked in Ireland." He went to Ire- land, he said, to protest against the action taken by the Government against William O'Brien (cries of 'Bless him ")—wbo had not broken the law, but bad helped to hinder the eyictione,.which would have been a breaking of the law. He (Mr:Brunner) placed mercy above the law, and be went to Mitchelstown to stand up, ICI mercy, even if it were against the law. He described his I journey to Mitchelstown. the mee ing wbich took place there, and the way in which "the miserable institution of a Government reporter" was forced upon the meeting. The police forced their way through the people up to a certain point, when a person en the platform said, Those- fellows are near eneugh, stand firm." A policeman had no more right in a crowd than any other man, and he (Nfr..Brunner) maintained that this was a perfectly I.gal direction In give 'to the crowd. (Applause ) The attack upon the crowd was absolutely wanton, unprovoked, and brutal' The polite etruck upon the crowd. every blow telling with hideous cruelty; and very spee.iily sticks on both sides ap- peared, but it seemed to him there were no more men attacking the police than there were police.. Yet the police soon began to run. (Laughter.) He saw one man go out of the crowd and drop three policemen as neatly as possible (Laughter and applause.) Although a magistrate and a law-abiding man, he should like to shake hands with that man. (Hear, hear.) He was a lover of peace, but he thought it right to fight when it came to resisting cruelty. He was hit three times by stones which were being thrown at the police, but be was not hurt in the least. In his opinion the palice who were being stoned were not in such danger as would justify them in firing upon the people. The eight of a policeman•was al- ways an irritating thing to a number of Irish.nen, and what they ought to have done at Mitchelstown was to, bare kept the policemen away. The Crimes Act had been passed by the Government not so much to prevent crime on the part of the people of Ireland, hut to legalize murder on the part of the pollee. They had learned not to put implicit faith even in English police- men (applause) but be had learned most thoroughly to nut no trust whatever in an Irish policeman —(anolanse)—eenecially when he was going through "swear drill." The inquiry was now going on Into this affair. but if the coroner' S jury brought in a verdict of wil- ful murder against a polic.esnan the Irish people had no guarantee that anything would come of it. And yet the Tories asked them to obey law and order when they paid no respect to law and order themselves. He urged upon Englishmen to go to Ireland and attend the meetings, be. Cause it bad a calming efNet upon Irishmen; an English- man brought with him a breath of air that dispersed the inflammable gases in the Irish atmosphere, which would create an explosion. Let them go to Ireland to protest for those who were now downtrodden, and for the rights which Englishmen now owned for themselves (Applause) Mr. C. P. Scott seconded the resolution, which was carried.

CAPTIMED BY BRIGANDS. An announcement that Mr. T. V., Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division of South-West; Lancashire had met with a somewhat romantic adventure during his tour in southern Europe occasioned considerable interest and excitement throughout the division he represents. in the House of Commons, during the earlier-part of the present week and the fact that lie escaped without any personal injury has given great satisfaction to his constituents. According to a Central News telegram from Vienna, on .Monday, news had arrived there that morning frons Sofia to the effect. that Mr. Thomas Wodehouse Legh, M.P., had been the subject of a sensational adventure, which had, however, fortu- nately terminated without worse results than tem- porary inconvenience to the hon. gentleman. It appears that last week Mr. oConor, the English consul at Sofia, his wife, and 3.1,r. Legh made an ex- cursion together to visit the monastery of Rib, which lies in a mountainous. region some forty or fifty miles south of Sofia. After spending some tin:where, Mr. Legh, who is a great lover of sport, went out alone to enjoy some shooting in the moun- tains. Whilst so engaged he was surprised by a band of brigands, who immediately seized him and bore him off a prisoner. Mr. Legh, however, pre- serving a wonderful coolness and presence of mind, represented himself as a, domestic servant, and so well did he act his part that the robbers were to- tally deceived. Believing that there was no pros- pect of obtaining a bounty for his release, and being fortunately too humane to summarily shoot a use- less prisoner, they Set him at liberty, and Mr. Legh quietly returned to Rib o without further molesta- tion. He rejoined Mr. O'Conor and the other mem- bers of his party, and all returned safe and sound to Sofia on Sunday. Commenting upon the incident a London corres- pondent remarks :—" Lancashire men will be inter- ested in the romantic story, reported on Monday night, of Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division. Mn Legh is the son of Mr. IV. J. Legh, who sat for many years for South Lancashire and East Cheshire, and he is heir to the magnificent es- tate of Lyrne, near Disley. Those brigands let a good chance slip, and I congratulate 111 r. Leigh on his adroitness. lie evidently did not serve five, years in the diplomatic service for 1,2"'

I WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING.

IThe annual general meeting of the members of the Warrington Musical Society was held in the school-room, Cairo-street, on Thursday evening. In the absence of the chairman (Mr. John Rylands), who, it was stated, was at present residing at his house near Llandudno, the chair was taken by Mr. P. Pearce, one of the vice-presidents of the society. There was not a large attendance.
SECRETARY'S REPOBT.
The IIoN. SEC. (Mr. L. Reyrkolds) read his report aa follows:

At the general meeting held in September, 1886, there was among the menhers present an all but unanimous de- eire that Handel's oratorio, Judas Maccabous." should be again performed, having been last given on December 16, 1874, and the committee accoalingly arraneed to include the work in the programme for 1886-7 ; it was, however, decided to deviate from the course hitherto usually adopted, and to reserve the oratorio for the second concert of the sea- son. For the first concert, given December 22, 1886, Cuwen's new cantata The eleening beauty " was selected. K 141.1 a short work by Costa, "The dream," previously given by the society (March 30th. 1880), the programme being made up with three songs, a trio, a chorus, and two instru- mental pieces by tbe splendid band engaged for this occasioneconsisting of 21 professional instrumental- ists, nearly all of Mr. C. Halle's orchestra. The vocalists engaged were Mrs Macon, Mr. Etward Kemp, and Mr Frank May, the cantralto solos being taken with great succese by Mee Monks, of Warrington ; the harp accom- paniments were given by Mr. T. R. Ford, hon. harpist to the society,. end the choruses were effectively rendered by the seciety's chsir of 100 voices. Toe production of " Judas Maccabeus " toot: place on March 16, 1887, the principals being :Mils Lillie, and Mies Jessie Marshall-Ward, Mr. Jeer McKay. and Mr. James Whittaker ; the band consisted of 16,professional instrumentalists, and the chorus of about 100 'members of the society. Both concerts, and all reheareals, were conducted by Dr. Hiles, who has now filled the post of conductor to the society for 22 seasons, and Mr. William Johnson discharged his duties as hon. organist with great ability and success. Mr. W. S. Woods again conducted an elementary sing- ing class in co•nection with the society. It is satisfactory to note that the socielr's choir has fully maintained its position, both as regards numbers and effici- ency, and that the subscription list of the past season was very nearly equal to the average of the six preceding years. The sale of tickets at the concerts realised rather less than in the two previous seasons, but at the oratorio concert the recPipte were in excess of the corresponding concerts in 1884.5 and 1885 6, probably owing to the efforts of certain members of the choir woo on this last occasion sold gallery tickets to the value of £4 10s. It has, however, during the peat three years become increasingly evident that the in- come of the society is insufficient to allow of its concerts being in all respects up to the standard of exczllence that is desirable, far the cost of a fairly complete orchestral band is so serious that strict ecenomy in the engagement of vocal- ists has become absolutely necessary, and it was a great disappointment to the committee when arranging for the petformance of "Judas," that want of funds rendered it impossible to engage for all the solo poets vocalists of equal calibre. Might not subscrib.rs do something more than they have done to add to their number, and do they fully realize that, by anything they may do to strengthen the society, they benefit themselves? Is it to be supposed that the town of Warrington cannot afford two first-class con- certs a year, and, if it can, would it not be to its credit to do so? The committee suggest that the lady members of the Society should form a committee among themselves during the ensuing season with a view to further the interests of the society.
