Mr. REYNOLDS, who is also hon. treasurer, sub- mitted the statement of accounts, which showed that the income of the past year was from subscrip- tions £l4O ss, tickets (first concert) £lO Os 6d, (scond concert) £l9 3s 6d, programmes (first con- cert) £3 2s 4d, (second concert) £3 is lid, hire of stage 10s, total receipts £176 12s 3d. The total ex- penditure amounted to £lBl Bs, a deficiency being thus left of £4 16s 7d. The balance due to the treasurer at the commencement of the season was £6 17s 6d, and when to this was added the deficit of .£4 16s 7d on the year 1886-7, there was a total balance against the society of .£ll 14 id.—On the motion of Mr. G. WALLINGTON, seconded by Mr.. HOWARD, the report and statement of accounts were adopted.

ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The CHAIRMAN proposed that Mr. Joint Rylands be re-elected president of the society.—M3e.Slswenis remarked that Mr. Rylands had been president about sixteen or seventeen years, and helesked hovr it would be to have a change. He thought they should have some new blood, and he suggested that Sir Gilbert Greenall might be elected president. (Laughter).—The CHAIRMAN said he did not think they would find any one more useful as a president than Mr. Rylands.—Mr. SEWARD said he would pro- pose that Sir Gilbert Greenall be elected president- -The Hon. SEC. asked if Mr. Seward knew-whether • Sir Gilbert Greenall would be ready to stand.--Mr. • SEWARD: I believe he will.—The propositiothof Mr. Seward was, however, not seconded, and. that of the chairman that Mr. Rylands be re-elected was agreed to.—As vice-presidents the following gentle- men were re-elected, viz.:—Messrs. J. Marson, W. Beamont, C. White, J. White, F. Monks, and P. Pearce. The hon. sec. was also elected a vice-presi- dent.—Mr. (1 WALLINGTON proposed that Messrs_ R. Fairclough, Dinwiddie, D. Garnett, Newcome„ Price, and J. P. Reynolds be re-elected to form. the committee.—Mr. E. Wallington said that with the- greatest respect he should like to make the state- ment that there had been a lot of complaints- amongst subscribers, ticket holders, amlthe general public that the performance of "Judas Afaccabeus"" had been too much hurried through. People said that it was because the conductor wanted to get away by a certain train, but he (Mr. Wallington) thought it would, have' been better to-wait till a. later train if they could have had a holler produc- tion of "Judas Maccabeus." He. thought if the committee was properly lormed they would see after these things in future.— Dr. limEs (who was present) said that "Judas, Maccabees" was done as fully as it is usual to do. it. The last part of the work was considered by most people to be inferior to the rest. If the com,-- plaint was that the movements were takert•too fast that was a matter for him to judge, and if therewas any censure he was afraid he should-hardly be in- clined to submit to it. (Laughter.)-Mr. E. VirAL- LINGTON repeated that there had been serious corn- plaints as to the hurried manner in which "Judas Maccabees" was performed, and if Dr. Hiles had nct heard of them before, he happened to be the man to inform him. He thought that a man hold- ing a public position like that of Dr. Hiles should know of the complaints that are being made.—Dr. RILES said that in his opinion the oratorio was. rendered at the proper rate, and the concert ended at twenty minutes to 10 o'clock, which was. as late as any concert ought to end, and was as late as the concerts in Manchester were intended to end. If it was with regard to the speed of the movement that complaint was made, then he must take- leave ta doubt,wkether Mr. Wallington was a proper critic.. If, however, there was any desire to change the conductor he should meet them .at once in the' frankest possible manner, but if it was.simply the individual opinion of Mr. Wellington he should ask them to pass on to the next business.—Mr. E. WAL- LINGTON said he should not like Dr. Hiles to mis- understand him. He simply-said that there had been, a complaint in Warrington/ with regard to the way- the oratorio had been performed, and iftthe respon- sibility rested with the committee then-they might have something to say upon it, but Wit rested in. the hands of the conductor, then he (Mr. Walling- ton) had done with it.—Mr. W. JoiLerson said that the committee itself, and not Dr..lllles, fixed the portion of the oratorio that should be performed. Re himself had been at many performances of " Judas " at Manchester and elsewhere, and he had never heard it performed in its entirety. (Hear,. hear.)—The subject then dropped, and Mr. Dinwid- die referred to the defective attendance of some, members of the committee.—Ultitaately, however-,, the committee was re-elected. RESIGNATIONS OF SECRETARY AND erItGANIST. On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. E. WALLINZTON, Mr. lbeytiolds was unani- mously re-elected hon. secretary and treasurer,— Mr. Ituvxmosthanked the meeting for the com- pliment paid him, but said that, as he found his work etellMlliittillg upon him he hoped- the society would accept his resignation, of the offices named. —lt was consequently agreed, on the motion of the CHAIRMAN,. that Mr. Reynolds should be re-elected pro. tem., and a vote in recognition of Mr. Reynolds valuable services to the society was also passed. —Mr. Sectson was then re-elected assistant secre- tary.—The CnArnizsx said a letter had been re- ceived from Mr. Johnson, resigning jiis position as hon. organist to the society. They were all very much obliged to Mr. Johnson for the valuable ser- vices he had rendered in, his capacity of organist. (Hear, hear.)—After a short discussion, it was weed, on the motion of Mr. JOHNSON' seconded by Mr. NEwcomit, that Mr. Muir should be appointed hon. organist to the society. THE NEXT ORATORIO.

On a vote being taken a consideiab. le majority of the members present voted in favour of the ora- torio" Sampson" being selected for the next perfor- mance of the society, "Moses in Egypt" was the second favourite. This was all the business.

SOMETHING ABOUT HULL. JUVENILE THIEVES.—WiIIiam Cunningham (12), eon of William Cunningham, and William Fleming (10), son of Michael Fleming, 10, Dial-street, were charged with having THE OLD AND TEE NEW Cm. AN INTERVIEW WITU . stolen a silk handkerchief, the property of Joseph Craik, 37, Arplev-street. The lads took the handkerchief from a AN OLD CITIZEN. clothes line, pawned it, and with the proceeds went to the theatre. Cunningham,who had been on a previous occasion birched for another off ,t3ce,was ordered to be kept in custody until six o'clock, and to receive six strokes with the birch rod, and Flemieg was ordered to be kept in custody until six o'clock. Hull is one of the most important cities of the United Kingdom, and as a seaport ranks next to Liverpool and London. It is a quaint old place of crooked streets and 1 narrow lanes, whose origin reaches back to the musty old days of tradition, and is somewhat shrouded in mystery. Certain authorities hold that the city was founded by Ed- ward I. in the year 1296; while others claim that by refer- ence to ancient records and authentic documents, it can be proved that it existed for upwards of a century before the time of that monarch, as a place of considerable commer- cial importance. Whether the latter view as to its origin is correct or not, it is certain that its progress was so great that in the reign of Edward :11. it was able to supply six- teen ships and five hundred men towards an armament for the invasion of France. The importance of this statement is realised when it is known that upon the same occasion the City of London furnished only tittnty-five ships and seven hundred men. Yet, however much her ancient im- portance may be questioned, there is no doubt as to the present commercial Importance of the city. Progress is seen on all sides. The sites of ancient fortifications are now occupied by docks and streets, and even the old citadel, which existed for centuries, has been swept away by the march of commercial improvements.

Within ten minutes walk cf the very centre of this scene of commercial life, at 23, Barleigh-street, Holderness-road, is the home of Mr. aeorge Woodhead, who for the past forty-one years, has been a resident of Hull. Mr. Wood- head is a shipbuilder by trade, and for the last twenty-six years has been constantly employed in the Drilling Depart- ment of the Earle Shipbuilding Co. As a man so long and intimately connected with the shipbuilding business could not help but have something of interest to say, we called at Mr. Woodhead's house, stated the obiect of our visit, and were courteously invited to take a seat. "Mr. Woodhead, I have been informed that for the past twenty-six years you have been an employ 6 of the Earle Shipbuilding Co." "Well, that's not exactly true. I have not been
employed by the company since 1834, bat for twenty. Aix-years previous to that time I was constantly employed there." _

"What was the reason for your stopping work 2" "The state of my health compelled me to. Up to three years ago I was very stout and rugged and hardly knew what ill-health was. At that time I began to pass blood with my water, which gradually increased in quantity, and was accompanied by a frequent and irritating desire with great straining. I kept at my work for a while, but was finally obliged to knock off." "I suppose you consulted your medical man ?" " Oh, yes; but he was unable to help me, and I grew worse, until I became seriously 11l from the eon- ant drain on my system that I was obliged to take to my bed."

" What did the doctors say was the cause of your trouble ? " :They said it was due to stone in the kidney, and that the oni; method of cure was to go to /he hospital and have it cut out." That was indeed a serions matter. Did you go to the hospital ?" " No, sir. Being well advanced in year; I doubted if I could survive the shock of so serious an operation, 85 I pre- ferred to die a natural death." "Then you never expected to get well? " "Indeed, I did not. I was so near gone that ray pulse could not be felt at the wrist, and I made all arrangements, so far as possible, for my death, even to selecting the pall- bearers!'

"But ilOw about your recovery? " " Well, while lying in an apparently hopeless condition, a friend brought me a bottle of Warner's SAF)I Cure, and as my doctors said they could do nothing more for me, I stopped all their medicines, and went to taking Warner's SAFE Cure."

Mr. Woodhead has lived in Hall the greater por- tion of his life, and is well-known to the inhabitants as a man of good standing whose statements can be relied upon." " It is really a remarkable case, is it not, Mr. Newton ? " "Yes, but there are others equally as wonderful. Why, It's only a few weeks ago that one whole page of the papers here in Hull was filled with tuts statements of our people, attested by t'seir facsimile signatures, as to the marvellous effects of the medicine. Its sale is steadily increasing, and no wonder, as such testimony must be convincing even to the moat sceptical."—Wetherby lirezes,Sept. 15.

THEATRICAL LIBEL ACTION AT WARRINGTON. At the- Borough Police Court, on Monday, a case neri. e before the borough mdgistrates, by adjourn- ment kin Saturday, which is of some interest to theatrical cf:nles. It was one in which Captain Frank Howard Dudley Ward, an actor appearing under the name of Captain Frank Dudley, charged Richard W. Steele, adVance ape of the "Sister Mary" Company, now touring, with having, on the 10th mat, published a defamatory libel concerning him. Prosecutor is a member of Mr. Duni); "Sus- picion" Company, that last week fulfilled an en. gagement at the Public When the UM first before the magistrates, on Saturday, Mr. P. Davies, who appeared for the prosecutor, said that previous to March last the prosecutor, who was for- merly in the Dragoon Guards and the Cape Mounted Rifles, had a company, of which defendant was a member. As it was not a success, the members, when at Blackburn, agreed to take a minimum sum as wages. Since that time the defendant had carried out a system of sending libellous post cards to the prosecutor, and on the day named in the charge prosecutor received one at the Public Hall, and his employer, Mr. Duval, also received a letter from the Idefendant, which was a libel on the prosecutor. The post vard,which the prosecutor received immediately on his arrival in Warrington, read as follows Captain (Ha-ha!) F. H. Dudley, "Suspicion Com- pany," Public Hall, Warrington.-46, Merrion-st., Leeds, September 10th. Please send me the 30s you owe me, balance of salary. You have got a good nerve to advertise when you cannot pay your debts. I shall run over to see you shortly. Remem- ber I had to pawn my ring to leave that swindle you got up in Blackburn. It is there now. One of your victims, RICHARD W. STELE. I have written Mr. Duval letting him know who and what you are." The letter was as under:—" Sister Mary Company, Grand Theatre, Leeds, September 10th. Dear sir.— You have in your company a man styling himself Captain F. H. Dudley. By his faulty education and bearing I have my doubts of the Captain,' and I know him to be what is termed a theatrical swind- ler. He engaged me last March to play in his wretched company—put me to endless expense in telegrams and much inconvenience in leaving hur- riedly all the way from Chatham to Blackburn, and at the end of three weeks I had to pawn my ring, &c., to pay my way and return to London. I have since seen the gallant Captain had had a Company again out, with, I hear, the same result as he had me. I have written him several times—my letter always being unanswered. I then began a system of post cards, and received two lawyer's letters threatening me. I wrote Dudley's lawyer asking him to commence his action, heard nothing more. I now see Dudley is with you; so that you may know who and what he is I write you this. I am the son of an old actor, sir, and a nephew of Mr. Fletcher, Theatre, Royal, Cardiff, and am pretty well known in the profession, therefore I think it only right to expose this man, if I may be allowed the ex- pression.-Yours respectfully. RICHARD W. &Timm"- Mr. Davies added that if the defendant would amply apologise for his conduct, and would pay all costs, his client would withdraw the charge.— Alderman Burgess said that the Bench thought , that the post-card in itself was a serious libel; he thought that the suggestion of Mr. Davies was a reasonable one.—Defendant: What I have said is true. If to speak the truth is libellous I am at fault.—lt was finally arranged that the case should be adjourned till Monday, bail being accepted in defendant's surety of .£5O, to allow him to then pay the costs. At Monday's court, Mr. Davies, address- ing the Bench, said that the defendant had made a full and ample apology, and was willing to pay all costs, including the insertion of the apology in the newspapers and under these circumstances he asked that the case against the defendant should be withdrawn. This course was agreed to. •

ALLEGED MURDER ON THE HIGH SEAS.—At the Liver- pool Police Court, on Thursday morning, before Mr. Raffles. a negro, named George Washington, was charged with mur- der on the high seas, on the the sth August last. A sailor on board theship proved doling the deceased stabbed. The prisoner, who was remanded, said he killed the deceased in self.defance, or he would have killed him. A MAN AND WOMAN DROWNED AT SALFORD.—An inquest was held at Salford, on Tuesday, on the body of a middle- aged man and woman, named Holt and Boyle, whese bodies were found in a canal on Sunday. The evidence showed I that the couple had lived together for several years, but had lately been separated. On Saturday night they were heard quarrelling on the canal hank, both of them being drunk.and on Sunday their bodies were discovered in the water. The supposition is that the woman fell into the water, and that the man lost his life in trying to rescue her. LIBRARY CONFERENCE. To tenth anngal conference of the Library Asscciation of the United Kingdom opened on Tuesday morning at Birmingham. under the presidency of Alderman Johnson, chairman of the association. The mayor welcomed the members, numbering over 150, and the president delivered an address on the progress of tree libraries and the important service they rendered in the education of the country. He pointed out the need of further developments, especially in the direction of assis- ting the studies of young people after school yeatS.

THE WARRINGTON LIBRARY. Sir,—l have watched with very great interest the ling struggle to make the Warrington Library what it should long age have been, a Free Lending Library, and I must confess to some surprise that the citizms of Warrington have so long permitted themselves to ho doubly taxed if they wished to borrow books from the Library. Ido not know of any other place in the United Kingdom where the free library has been ao restricted in its use as that in your town, and commencing as it did at such an early date it was really incumbent on the committee to have hang ago placed themselves in line with all the free libraries in the country worth the name. For some time prior to the answer of the Attorney- General in the souse of Commons, I have looked upon the subscription method for borrowers as illegal, and Ido not I think that any free library committee need be dismayed at his expression of doubt as to whether it is legal to lend books at all. The "reasonable deposit to ensure their safe return " where they are lent, to which the Attorney- General referred, Is practically and absolutely covered by I the vouch-r signed by a burgess for the borrower. There is no trouble in getting these vouchers signed, and there is little risk when they are signed. At Cheltenham, during the lait lilwary year, out of a total of 203,177 vols, issued liot a single Look was unaccounted, for, and the percentage of less is not more than one in 30,000 volumes issued. With an income of over £5OO a year from the rate, War- rington ought unquestionably to be a Free Lending Library. Quite a long list of libraries could be mentioned which have a large lending issue daily on a smaller income than this. At Walsall, with an income of £520, the daily average is over 210 vols, in the lending department. A Public Library established under the Acts is not a rate- payers' institution where books are lent out to be read to those who can afford to pay the subscriptioa, and denied to tkose who cannot, or will not, on principle, pay this addi- tional tax illegally levied by the committee. I have been always reluctant to Interfere with the inner working at any library, but I would earnestly appeal to the committee to set themselves right on this matter. Free Libraries have now reached the critic.] stage, and opponents of the movement in other places are making capital out of Warrington not being able, they say, to pay its expenses oat of the rate, but has to tax its borrowers to make up the deficiency. A statement such as this carries greater weight in a public meeting than the committee of the Warrington Library would, perhaps, acknowledge, and as the friends of the movement have no desire to forge bullets for their oppo- nents. it will be impossible to any longer include Warring- ton among the Free Public Libraries of the country, if the present method is continued. This is a reading ages, and every facility should be given for citizens to read at home rather than placing obstacles in the way of their doing so. I would ask in all reasonable- ness whether, out of over 23,000 volumes, an issue of some 130 a day is at all commensurate with such a stock and such an outlay in money? Libraries with one half the number of books are issuing double the number per day. So that on the score of getting value for money the citizens of War- rington should insist on the freeing of the library. The day for restrictions on education is past, and Free Libraries can reasonably claim to be educational institutions. As a Cheshire man I would like to see my native county, with Lancashire and Yorkshire, taking the lead in all move- ments for the public good, and whilst there Is this stigma against what should be a very prominent Free Library this is impossible so far as this movement is concerned.—Yours faithfully,

RUGBY RULES. WIDNES RECREATION Y. POOLSTOCH (WIGAN) —Played at Widnes on Saturday. Score :—Recreation, two goals and six minor points ; Poolstock, two minor points. Mc- Cririe and Hewitt scored the tries. Barker improving upon them. WIDNES Y. WlGAN.—These teams, both well represented, mat at Wigan on Saturday, in the presence of 3,0(10 spec- tator', many of whom had journeyed from Widnes. and a fine and well-contested game resulted in a victory for Wid- nes by one goal, one try, awl nine minors, to ens goal and eight minors. Widnes played with the wind in the first half, and quickly added half a dozen miners. On two oc- casions they looked like scoring, the forwards dribbling across the Wigan line, but each time they sent the ball dead by kicking too hard. At last, however, when in the Wigan half, Parkinson picked up cleverly and dropped the ball over the bar in splendid style. Shortly afterwards Plump' on kicked well. Wilkinsoe followed up, and carried the ball to the line, where he lost it. and Hughes rushed ie and secured a try near the posts. Farrell failed to improve mat- ters. Even with the wind against them, the visitors showed better play than Wigan, and it was not until about a quarter of an hour from the call of time, when Slevin dropped a fine goal, that the horn. team appeared to advan- tage, and then their fierce attacks were repelled by the Wid- nesians, and the game closed as above stated. Both behind and in the pack Widnes were the superior team, their quick loose play defeating the ponderous tactics of the Wiganites. September 19th, 1857. MR. ROBERT D.AVIES AND THE FREE LIBRARY. Sir,—l notice that Mr. Robert Davies has written one of your contemporaries on the subject of the Warrington free library. Perhaps I ought rather to say that the free library question is the ostensible subject of his letter, for after reading the epistle it seemed that its real purpose was to illustrate and enforce the proposition which be himself lays down, that "arguments have the awkward property of possessing two edges." Take, for instance, his own argu- ment that many of the books in the library are already " well worn, and many are still in boards, unbound, and considerable expense would have to be incurred• to fit them for much wear anA tear." This argument is apparently intended to tell against the scheme for freeing the library, because if the library were free these books would be more used, but that is only one of the edges of the argument. It possesses another edge, and cuts another way, for if these tender volumes are "already well worn," the way to preserve them is not by keeping the library as it is, but by making it still more ex' elusive, or better still, by closing it altogether, except to nice refined gentlemen like Mr. Davies, who are warranted to have clean soft hands.—Youre, _

_ The Orient steamship Iberia left Plymouth shortly after noon on Saturday with the two teams of English cricketers on board. All the members of Shrewsbury's team, except Mr. Smith and balf-a-dozen of Mr. Vernon's side, joined at Plymouth. On Saturday a 15 miles bicycle match for a stake of £25 a side was decided on the North Shields Bicycle Track, between W. Wood and R. H. English, in the presence of some 5,000 spectators. The contest was a fairly interesting nature, but eventually Wood won rather easily by ten yards in 50min. 44 1-ssec. The St. Helens Recreation Club provided an attraction on Saturday afternoon, when the famous Kendal Hornets were their opponents. The home team had secured the assistance of two Runcorn and one Aspull players, and the generally expressed anticipation of an exciting game was realised. The home team was warmly applauded, and the result of the struggle—a win for the Rees by several points—was a very popular one. The St. Helens (Rugby) Club, on Saturday, bad as their " guests" the Werneth team' and the latter succeeded in defeating the Denton's Green fifteen. Owing to the Kendal Hornets v. Rees attraction, the attendance was considerably under the average, and the play, too, seemed to be below the usual standard of the St. Helens men. The visitors secured the match by 1 goal, 1 try, and 5 minors, to 1 try and 4 minors. The Earlestown Association Club got a nice " drop " on Saturday, when both the first and second (or "reserve ") teams sustaived serious reverses at the hands of the Newton Heath contingent. A season or two ago the Earlestown Club in one season beat Newton Heath by eight goals to none, and four goals to none respectively in two matches. but this cannot be repeated at present. The Newton Heath has prgressed witb rapidity, and now boasts the possession of one of the best teams in the county. The match between the second elevens resulted in the defeat of the Earlestown 2ed by four goals to one. The St. Helens Association Club had a fixture last Satur- day with the Southport Old Boys, who were runners-up for last season's Southport and District Challenge Cup. The match was played at Southport, and proved an exciting and hard•fought affair. At one period in the first halt St. Helens held a lead of three goals, but the seasiders gradu- ally drew level. Neither team again scored, and the match was thus drawn. Sims, late of Earlestown, played a splen- did game for the-visitors.

THE FREE LENDING LIBRARY QUESTION' INN—It is satisfactory to see, that with the coming win- ter the Free Library Question is again to the front. I have been at some tronble, just to satisfy myself, in hitherto, g eithern p the p uvariousbiciy or privately spoken unfavourably members of the Council who have of the scheme, and I have come to this opinion about them, —they know uotbing of the charm that is added to domes- tic life through the circulation of books in the home circle. Of course, I am well aware that Mr. Reamont and a few more of his school know the value of books, but may it not partake so much of the antiquarian, and old-world type as to be injurious rather than beneficial to the present age? It is not in the nature of things that these gentlemen should know the powerful forces now at work impeding the British workmen in their struggle to hold their own, nor yet is it possible for the opponents to the movement, at present in the Town Council, to thoroughly grasp the situation. The present writer knows as a fact that the chief opponents in the council are men who pride them- selves on having made their way In the world " without ony book learning." Mr. I3eamont, and those who think with him, ahould know that we want cheap literature for two reasons. First, we want it because we know that it is the most powerful elevating infleence that can be introduced into the home circle, that unless the parents have, unfortunately for them- selves, net been trained to read and study, there is an in- I difference betrayed in their everyday life as to their duty as parents, and as to their duty as citizlns, the result of which makes itself manifest by higher rates for the repression and control of the criminal classes We are anxious to make the reading of a book a greater pleasure to a young man or woman than the standing at street corners or attending a singing saloon. It is by the acceptance of this principle in Germany, and I may say throughout the continent, that we are now being worsted in foreign labour centres.

No objection has yet been made that is a credit to the objector. If only money is required, then I say it ought to be forthcoming, or the labourers of Warrington have labeured for the eurichm.nt of a thankless lot of employers. It may be, and I know it is with a few, that they dread see- ing, or touching a book that is a little soiled. Bless us all! Such squeamishness does not enter into young ladies' heads when they coolly take books out of the library for which the workmen have already paid a penny rate. As a matter of I fact, in comparison with Manchester, Liverpool, Newcastle, and other large towns, the cost for books soiled, spoiled, Jrc, is greatest in the Warrington rate-aided subscription library, sometimes called the Free Library. In other towns the art izan class are more careful of the books than are the select classes in Warrington. The Mayor has called a Town's Meeting for Tuesday even- ing. I hope the town's people will mark their sense of its importance by crowding the Co-operative Hall. "ON THE JOB."

THE CONTROL OF DOGS, Sir,—May I be allowed, through the medium of your valuable columns, to state that I consider it the duty of the local authorities, and of the Government, to take means to lessen the annoyance, danger, and injury to the public caused by rabid and other dogs. I have noticed five deaths in Lancashire, within two months, from hydrophobia, and the deaths from hydrophobia are only a small portion of the injury caused by dogs being allowed to wander through the streets and country unmuzzled, and without anything Ito indicate to whom they belong. It is a great disregard of social order and of justice to allow individuals to keep animals that are so often an annoyance, danger, and injury to the public, and practically to be so little responsible for the injury they may do. It is the duty of individuals who keep dogs for pleasure or use to take means to prevent them annoying or injuring the public, and it is the duty of local authorities and the Goverment to see that these conditions are enforced. The most contemptible mongrel car, if afflic- ted with rabies, may, by a little scratch upon the hands or face, cause the death of the most beautiful woman or the strongest man, and their last hours to be almost horrible, that otherwise might have been peaceful and happy, and we should protect our children from their poisonous or savage fangs. 7.5. KENYON. Warrington, September 22ad, 1887.

div.head: THE. GAS COMMITTEE AND CONTRACTS.
div.p: THE. GAS COMMITTEE AND CONTRACTS.

Sir,—While looking over the doings of the Town Coun- cil at its lest meeting, I could not help thinking that it is about time the ratepayers were beginning to exercise their power of control if they do not wish to see their Corporation afllicted with two of the worst maladies which experience has shown that municipalities are liable to, namely, govern- ment by clique, and secrecy in monetary transactions. To me it seemed that the symptoms of these maladies were to be seen in the most unmistakable form in what took place over the minutes of the Gas Committee. Let us consider for a moment how matters stood. The Council at some previous meeting passed a resolution that the prices at which Corporatiorecontracte were accepted were to he pub- licly recorded on the minutes of the respective committees. In obedience to this resolution the other committees have. I believe, put the prices 01 the contracts recommended by them on their minutes; but no sooner does the Gas Com- mittee come to deal with tenders that must involve an ex- tremely large sum of money, than they disregard in the most open and contemptuous manner the directions of the Council, and hold to the old system of keeping contract prices dark, Here we have government by a secret irres- ponsible clique in full bloom. For why is it that the Gas Cimmittee ventured to act in this way contrary to the ex• pressed decision of the Council? Is it not because the committee is so strong that in all matters concerning its own department of the town's affairs it really controls the Council, while the Council has no cont-el over it? In an- swer to the protest of two or three members, Alderman 1 Holmes, the chairman of the committee, barely condescended ' to offer any explanation why the committee bad acted in a way which is, looked atin a proper light, an outrage on the , constitution of a corporation. It was, said Alderman Holm IS ' very briefly, considered to be for the interests of the public that the prices should not ba published. It will be seen that there is nothing novel about this explanation; it is the earns plea that has done service on behalf of every public abuse. But, at the same time, it raises the very important question as to who is to be the judge in corporation matters of what is aed what is not for the public interest. Is this judge to be the Council as a whole, or that portion of the Council which forms the Gal or any other Committee? The Council deliberates publicly, and the ratepayers have conse- quently a means of ascertaining and criticising, if need be, the reasons and arguments that lead it to any conclusion, but who knows what it is that influences a committee? Once let it be admitted that a committee which, so far as the general 1 public is concerned, conducts its proceedings in the most im- penetrable privacy can overrule the Council, and then we I have rvvroment by *responsible clique in Its most namiti- I gated form. I Warrington, Sept., 1887.

Sir,—l am obliged to you for inserting my letters on the above aubject, and although I appear to be attacking this matter single-handed, there are others biding their time, and will in due course have their say. I am welt aware that it

is a bold thing to attack officials, especially of long stand- ing; but if these officials have' erred, and are still deter- mined to err in the spending of the ratepayers' money, it protest must be made somewhere. Men must not be allowed to carry a hobby se far as to play fast and loose with up- wards of £20,000; and now want to play away with thou- sands more over the same fanciful scheme, which is sure to end in failure. lam supported by prominent men in the town when I say that far toe mach has been left to the chair- man of the Sanitary Committee and the borough surveyor in the matter of Longford and these depot schemes; for whichever way I trace it,and I have tried, I cannot see that there has been very much talent or experience exhibited in the whole transaction. This is clearly shown in the faulty beginnings, and in the bad calculation which has been made. The very tank which is now asked for, together with the large water cistern, were included in the last £13,000 raised; but the cost ea far exceeded the estimate that I suppose for the time being they were left over. But this tank we are told is for storing purposes. But why store it ? If the plant had been properly laid out according to the plans and estimates, the excreta would have been worked up as it was forthcoming, and no storage would have been required; and no man having the slightest experience in these matters would have engaged in either iron or steel tanks for the re- ception of this stuff, knowing its corrosive power. But why these two intercepting depots, when they have to be worked at different time? When Longford onlyeexisted, the whole of the excreta was taken there, and there was an end to it ; but when the two depots were erected their situa- tion compel,ed the vans to gather the pails from the very outskirts of the town, right through the centre of it, to these depots, in order to force it up to Longford. And in their ignorance, I find members of tho Town Council, and others, are under the impression that everything in these pails is forced up the pipes ' • and their great surprise to learn that at least one third of it has to be re-carted back through the town to places outside of it, to the great annoyance of the rural population (I am speaking now of' the depot this side Sankey Bridge), and the condemnation of the medical pro- fession. I have some damaging evidence in respect to this place, which at present I reserve. Now let us take the first intercepting depot—Battersby. 1 lane. At first there was a great difficulty in getting land ' for it on account of the probable nuisance; but it was at last secured, and £950 paid for it (I don't know whether the £l5O compensation to Mr. Alderman Holmes is included or not), but the land was let with the distinct understanding that there was to be no nuisance; therefore this proving a failure, it is not unlikely but that the town will be forced, to purchase the land adjoining, which would be a pretty mess, for who would build in such a place? Think over this, ye ratepayers; I thought you had had enough with the Bridge-street job. This very depot was erected without an immediate road to it, and a chained horse had to be kept in readiness (all expenditure) to assist in dragging the heavy vans into it; and, the becoming intolerable, a street had to be made at a cos l of over £3OO, which the town had to pay (through bad management), although private property existed on two sides of it. I only mention this to show that, in my opinion, a thorough meditated plan had not been considered. And now we take the Howley depot (and I wish anyone would spend either Friday, Saturday, Monday, or Tuesday in its vicinity, in order to pass judgement as to the nuisance), and there we find a large expenditure in road making; and ground. which is only worth a penny per yard, we ale pav- ing fourpence for; and the erection of one part of it is sim- ply a discredit to whoever had the management of it. All this, sir, is in addition to creating two plague spots in the town; and I will place my judgment in the hands of any practical man, and ask him whether any private firm would squander money away in this fashion? BLit in the face of all this blundering I find from the receipts and expenditure of the borough (a copy of which is before me) that a gra- tuity of £lOO is given for extra services rendered, and £73 3s for expenses for running about the country seeking in- formation; all this in addition to a salary of £4OO per year. Well may it be asked, " Why does not the Ratepayers' Asso- ciation grow ?" The question has often been asked, where is the engineer- ing skill that has been brought to bear in connection with, this scheme? The chairman of the Sanitary Committee certainly has none, and I think our borough surveyor cannot possibly lay claim to much, and the inspector, under•in- spector, exc., are almost nil. Therefore the failure cannot be wondered at. There is a breakdown at Longford, but no one can get at the bottom of it. The work could not be done in the day time as calculated, and night work had to be resorted to; and as they could not afford to keep two competent men, it is hinted that the night man may have caused the breakdown. I hope this will be brought home at the proper time. In conclusion, sir, the question we, the heavy-burdened ratepayers. have to ask is, "Is it true that when this great sanitary scheme was first introduced that we had, abet have still, a practical engineer in our town, who offered to erect and carry the scheme out, work it solely in the day time, personally superintend it, and guarantee its success to the town for £2,000 less than the estimated cost at the time?" This latter is the most serious of all, and should be inquired into by all.—Yours truly,
WILLIAM DIG GLE. 19, Wellington-street, September 21, 1837.

- THE CONTINENTAL WORKMAN. Sir,—ln‘oontinaation of the above subject, allow me to draw your readers' attention first to the enormous magni- tude of continental commerce. I am afraid the Eng- lish workman has no conception of what is going on abroad, but fancies that England and her workshops are to-day what they were in the past, the wonder and admiration of the world. Of course lam aware that I run the great danger of being called unpatriotic, should I dare to place other countries in comparison with my own, my native laud; but let us workmen know the facts and face them. I take the continental workman as representing the lowest depth to which it is sought to bring English workmen, and to know how likely. he is to achieve this object,we must know what he is doing. Westphalia alone has a magnificent bituminous coalfield producing over twenty million tons of coal per annum. The Gilchrist modification of the Bessemer process for convert- ing iron into steel is in more general use than in any other part of the world. In Belgium are situated the largest zinc works in the world. This firm—the Vielle Montavne Com- pany—employ 7,500 workpeople, distributed over 18 mines and smelting works. Their mines annually supply them with 70,000 tons of minerals of various kinds. The total indicated horse power of their engines is 5,000. The total of the zinc prodacts of the world amounts to 236,000 tons per annum; of this amount the continent produces 196,000 tens, England 25,000,and the United States 15,000 tons. One more instance—that of the Cockerill Society, at Seraing,near Liege, founded by a Lancashire man in 1817. At that time the town of Seraing had a population of 2,000, it is now 50,000. The works cover over 250 acres, and give em- ployment to over 16,000 men, to whom £4OOOOO a year are paid in wages. The company possess 280 stationary engines, with motive power equal to 12,000 horses. They consume 1,000 tons of coal and coke per day, and produce locomo- tives, stationary engines, bridges, boilers, iron ships, and general machinery. These works stand unrivalled through- out the world for the variety of their productions. I must pass over Krupp's works in Westphalia, the factory of La Creazot in France, both firms having been recently well described in the papers. It only remains for me to add that I could place before your readers descriptions of works of almost similar magni- tude in the cotton, woollen, and braiding trades, scattered all over Germany, France, Switzerland, and Italy. Without this, I think your readers will fully grasp the enormous magnitude of the capital and labour engaged in the compe- titive struggle. And what of labour ? What is to be its ultimate reward in the death struggle now going on ? A writer in the " Standard " recently said, "It is not too much to say that if the poor would eat horse or donkey enormous social dangers that now seem inevitable would disappear." I have described the works at Seraing; they are splendid monuments of what can be done with exploit- ing labour; bat what of the labourers? Acm respondent of the "Times "says : "They have to live chiefly on dry bread, black, bitter, rye-bread. On Sundays they may get a little meat or sausage, the latter made of pork or horse flesh. At Seraing four horses are slaughtered weekly for this purpose, the animals so killed being described as being "old, decrepid, tough, but not diseased," their flesh being "wholesome, but not nasty." I think your readers will agree with me that if this is the "level of the world " to which we are to come, it would be worth while to make an effort to avert it. There may be a lower depth still in the following : "In the Charleroi district little girls go into the pits and take their share of the rough work with the boys. Many of them continue at this through life." This needs no comment. It is only want of room forbids use going more into the continental workman's condition, and not want of mate- rial. Let us look at the Italian. At Brillu, the " Mane cheater of Italy," there is no Factory Act ; children begin to work at eight years of age, and from eight to ten are paid from 44 to 7d per day, curd feeders, women, Is per day; dyers, Is 63 ; weavers (by piece), from 9d to Is Gd per day ; everlookers from 23 3d to 3s 3d per day. Even with these low wages and cheap water power they "do not dream of competing with England." The employers at the largest works in Brilla have turned a disused mill into is kind of model cottages, 'through which some visitors were conducted. " Ire one dwelling of two rooms, a little girl of four or five years:of age was nestling, close to a small fire of sticks and tending a cooking pan that was over the fire. The mother was busily occupied in arranging the room. We were taken into the bedroom, and our attendant, the woman who acted as caretaker of the block, pointed with 901113 enthusiasm to a baby wrapped la swaddling clothes on the bed. She told us that at was but three days old, and that the busy housewife whom we had seen at work in the next room was its mother." One more example of how they do things in the land with which we are engaged in competitiota. Going into the north of Italy we find a very different state of things to what obtain in Germany. Education is neglected, and is too un- popular to become compulsory. Factory work is associated. The wages paid are fixed without any consultation with the labourer. " The most highly paid receive about Is 2d per day, and 5d a day is considered good pay for children. Bread and soup is provided, with dormitories for sleeping. "So that from Monday morning to Saturday night there is no necessity for any of the workpeople to leave the pre- mises." What is the life of these wretched workers may be guessed. "1 he beds consisted of mattresses, with, in many instances, the straw protruding. There were no sheets, but for each bed a rug and a quilt. Washing utensils and looking glasses there were none. Our conductor informed us that at ten o'clock at night, when the engines stopped the women and children without any delay hasten to their beds. They have no inclination for wasting time over their toilets. They throw their tired limbs upon their trestle beds, and without undressing, sleep till they are, warned at 4=45 next morning that they must be up again and prepare for their work." Sir, when we read that the most popular dish with these works is "bread sopped in warm water, with a pinch of salt" we are simply struck with amazement. Poor Italy ! her history is a sad super- stition and a melancholy one, but deserves attention from those more favourably placed. Your readers- must not fancy that I have picked out ex- ceptional cases. In this one district of Italy there are sixty- five silk factories, all similar in character. Bat there is something cheering to English workmen. There is a desire on the part of continental workmen to rise out of the degraded and unmanly serfdom in which they have hither- to been kept by employers. On all hands testimony is borne of the good resulting from "English workmen hav- ing been brought up en a mere liberal allowance of animal food than any of their continental rivals." Nowhere is the double shift system approved of. The manager of oae of the largest Belgian works said a He did not believe there was any advantage in 12 hours as worked on the con- tinent. over Pi worked in England. More work is done in England in 91 hours than is Belgium in 12 hours." I have before me evidence of this kind without stint, and not to be challenged. The conclusion to which it points is, that if the English land laws were reformed out of exis- tence, and its minerals and all other deposits, the accumu- lations of ages of nature's work were free to the people, and not personal property, England has not reached the height of her glory. But what should be her glory? Not simply competing with the continent, but taking the initiative in putting a stop to all labourers, whether English, French, German, or whatever nationality they own, from underselling their labour for mere competitions sake. To nationalise labour, and make the workers of all nations brothers, would be grand, and should ba genial work for Englishmen. The immigration of foreigners is a subject worth considering in an early letter.
CLIFFORD DIX.
ON THE TRACK OF THE SHIP CANAL.

(From the "Sunday Chronicle.") To Captain Aldred was entrusted the task of pilot- 1 ing your exploring party on their second expedi- • tion, which you will understand was strictly naval. I propose to take up my parable from below the meeting of the waters at Partington, the confluence of the Irwell and the Mersey, near where our pre- vious journey reached its outward limit. I find that our river boatmen do not apply the word" Mer- sey' to the incoming stream. It is invariably alluded to as "the Cheshire Watters " by these gentry, who are no respecters of maps or geography books. Some notion of the stupendous character of the Ship Canal Company's operations can be formed from the statement that from Manchester down to this point the river Irwell will presently have ceased to exist. With the exception of a Jew outlying curves, which will probably be allowed to silt up, or be artificially re-claimed, ,the whole of the river bed for eight miles will have been widened to a minimum breadth of 40 yards and deepened to 26 feet. Just below this pleasant patch of rural scenery the company's coal basins will be formed. in direct communication with the Glazebrook and Stockport Railway, part of the direct route from London to Liverpool. A little fur- ther down stream is the railway bridge by which the line now crosses the river. This will be removed and a high-level bridge substituted, with sufficient headway for large steamers to pass under. A considerkhle shifting of gradients will be invol- ved in the Pfocess, Which of course will have to be repeated wherever a line crosses the Canal. A pic- turesque farmstead, known as Rodger's Farm, is visible on the left bank, beneath the arches of the present bridge, and will vanish along with it when the new waterway is made. -Pushing onwards, we retie& another old landmark that will soon be swept away at Cadishead. This is the range of buildings used as stables by the old navigation company, when they regularly ran boats between Manchester and Warrington—a lingering relic of a traffic long since departed. As a matter of fact, the canals and the railways have long since extinguished the river as a profitable source of income to carriers, and any inquisitive voyager who chooses to follow the track of this journey of ours, will find that he has the Mersey pretty much to himself. Winding through a rich country, its banks overhung with willows and bordered by noble avenues of trees, a century old; each mile of progress opening up new perspec:- tives of sylvan landscape, flecked here and there with white-walled farmsteads and stacks of mel- lowing Imy.--This open sewer, upon which we are riding, seems like a filthy intruder upon polite soci- ety. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY NIGHT. There is just now somewhat of a scare at the prevalence of scarlet fever. The instances are not really so very numerous, but we have. become sud- denly so alive to questions of sanitation, that any infectious disease is looked upon as a quite unneces- sary evil. The four-wheel cab is really the great cause of the spread of these diseases. And the difficulty is for the friends of the patient to know what to do. During the small-pox scare, there were cabs painted yellow devoted to the service, and, of course, every fever hospital has one or two of these in its employ. I see that within the fortnight Paris has had to meet the same difficulty, and it has met it. On certain cab stands a vehicle may always be found for the transfer of an infected patient. The scale of charges is high, that is, it is more than double the ordinary tariff, but then, in the case of the poor, the hospital will do the work for nothing. Sooner or later the matter must be dealt with by our authorities. As it is the Chief Commissioner has shown a little activity in a mat- ter that slightly touches the subject. He has this season considerably increased the number of cab- stands. The step was not taken before it was needed. Every one admitted that crawling and loitering led to a majority of our street accidents, and that they should be suppressed. Indeed, since one of the city magistrates was knocked down by a car in Cheapside, a couple of years ago, the police have been much more industrious in seizing offen- ders. But if the cabs are not allowed to crawl they must go to their stands. The number of cabs increases each year, and so should the number of stands. But private influence is promptly brought to bear. Easy proximity to a cabstand, actually adds to the tell- ling value of a house, direct proximity very con- siderably diminishes it. The individual must suf- fer. He admits the proposition and tries to shift the individuality. Sir Savile Brinton-Crossley has at last been caught. ' We have a good many baronets, but we have very few who have £45,000 a year, and of these few very few, indeed, are 28, and unmarried. For the last couple of seasons Sir Savile has been one of the great catches of society. His place near Lowestoft, and his place near Halifax, his income, his appearance, and his age, were all that could be desired, and were all desired with a great deal of genuine avidity. At last this court card falls. I hear Miss Phyllis de Bathe takes the trick. She is the youngest daughter of Sir Henry de Bathe, whose troubles with Mrs Weldon excited amongst his friends a good deal of pity. I passed Scott's hat shop to-day, and looked in the window with considerable interest. In the shop itself was that assistant who makes the quartette of London "doubles." He is so like Lord Hart- ington that it is said the Duke of Devonshire might easily mistake somebody else's son for his own. The other three resemblances are a shade lower in the social grade. Two of them are waiters and one is a manager. The latter presides, or till recently used to preside, over the lunch takers at the Horse Shoe, in Tottenham Court-road. He was so obviously in command there that he could scarcely really be the Marquess of Salisbury. but he looked very like him. A more striking resemblance was that of the head waiter of the Cock to Roundel Palmer. Tennyson calls him the plump head waiter, but he never was plump. He ran his life parallel with the leading equity barrister, aged very much as and how he did, and seemed to gain in dignity when the other mounted the woolsack. The fourth is the head waiter at Simpson's, whose resemblance to Mr. Teignmouth Shore is most remaikable. Mr. Shore is an excel- lent preacher, but does not look as like a church dignitary as the waiter at the Cock looks like a legal light. But why I stopped at Scott's window was to see the brims of the new hats. There is a horrible report out that they are to be very broad— like a quaker's. The mode has actually already been introduced in Paris. lam happy to say that there are no symptoms of excessive brims either in that window or at Lincoln and Bennett's. I hear we are to have even yet another line to New York. The Atlantic will become quite danger- ous. And the strange thing is that none of the existing lines pay very well. And yet new vessels are ordered by two of the great Liverpool compan- ies, so as not to leave all in the hands of the Etru- ria and the Umbria. The new idea seems to take common sense into iticalculations. The vessels would run from Milford Haven direct to Sandy Hook. Queenstown would be disregarded. It is thought that some 20 hours should be saved on the run. Of course, passengers would choose the quick- est route. Their food for a day would be saved, and what is more important a day's coal would be saved. But lam told the idea is that the boats are to be merely for passengers. ‘The truth is there is a great waste of economy in conveying merchandise at so rapid a rate. The wheat and cotton, and other commodities, are in no such violent hurry. The new boats would certainly be smaller, but that need not affect their speed. The line can not be started till the present works at Milford are completed. At the rate things are going now the Thames will soon become almost invisible in the stretch of it that extends between London Bridge and Charing Cross. Railway interests take precedence of all others, and the very last thing that a Londoner thinks of is the beauty of his city. The bridge oder the river at Charing Cross is to be consider- ably widened, and the bridge at Cannon-street is to be made nearly twice as wide. The South Eastern, as a company, is not remarkable either for accom- modation or for punctuality. But the truth is un- punctuality mainly arises from the blocks and stops on the few furlongs of route between London Bridge and Cannon-street and Charing Cross. The Cannon-street station holds eight lines of rail under its ample rootage, but the bridge only accommo- dates three or four. The projected improvements will be of enormous value in making extra traffic not merely possible but easy. Perhaps also some- thing would be done with those miserable sheds curiously dignified with the name of London Bridge Station, In the meantime we are losing sight of the Thames. London may soon be des- cribed as built not on a river, but on railway bridges. The police are at last taking steps to put down a nuisance that has grown up gradually and has re- cently become intolerable. It is the nuisance of costermengers. The word is used technically and does not necessarily mean a man with a donkey harnessed to a cart full of goods. The costers now being dealt with consist largely of foreigners. They stand with a little tray'of goods just off the kerb- stone of the most crowded thoroughfares. Cheap- side is a favourite haunt. They manage their busi- ness very cleverly. As a rule the goods are all one price, say I?, penny or twopence each—watch keya, pencils, shirt studs, sleeve links, umbrella rings, as the case may be. The trade done is enormous. All profit, clear profit. The very best sites in the city of London are secured rent free. The costers • are actually. able to undersell ' the shops, so much time is saved in an out-of-door purchase. If the eases had been isolated,i the authorities would never have interfered. But latterly Cheapside became quite blocked, and at; Christmas time the nuisance was considerably aug- mented. One has a kind of pity for the costers, but the greatest good of the greatest numbers should also be considered. I hear on all sides of the deliberate pushing of German goods to the exclusion of our own manu- factures. The subject has become so serious, that many of our Consuls abroad have reported on it. It is not that our productions are inferior, but that the German work is cheaper, and the German organise- ' tion incomparably better. lam told that they are making great efforts to beat us out of the field at the forthcoming Exhibition at Melbourne. But it is the I same story everywhere, and especially in Southernl and Central America. We have been relying on our

name, while the Germans have set before them, to quote one of their own pamphlets, the duty of creating the demand Which they shall thems4ves be able to supply. It is a serious question for England. Trade runs in grooves, and if the channel turns out of our way we count, by and bye, to be able to turn it back. It is sad to think of the beautiful grounds at ,Lillie Bridge all in a ruinous condition. A heavy loss will fall on the company who owns them. The excitement was immense when the report went about that it was the American Exhibition that had caught fire. It is not likely the company will be compensated,as the mob had certainly some ground , for their fury. A little time ago one of those auto- matic boxes was found not in working order. A member of the British public had put in a penny and got out nothing. He and his friends smashed up the box, and found great enthusiasm and support in the crowd. There are cases when the executive ought not to interfere.

What was the feeling in England to-day? What was the feeling amongst them, and amongst the masses of the people? Why, if there had to be a general election to-morrow that party would be defeated, and the Coercion Bill would be swept away for ever. (Hear, hear.) They would not have the freedom of the Irish people trampled upon. He was speaking that day to his friend, Mr. Brun- ner—(cheers)—and Mr. Brunner told him that he attended a meeting at Bantry last Sunday. The police came to the priest who was going to act as the chairman, and said—" Will you guarantee that the Government reporter shall have a seat?" "Certainly," was the reply. "he shall have a seat." The reporter went to the meeting between two priests ; there was no disturbance, and no need for a policeman. There was not one to be seen. Was not that a contrast to the disgraceful scene at Nlitchelstown ? Thank heaven there were two English members who could tell the English peo- in the House of Commons the truth about what took place there. (Cheers.) Mr. Balfour, in the House of Commons, made a statement that was simply a report given to him by an official in Ireland, and a report which he (Mr. Crosfield) did not hesitate to say was a tissue of falsehoods from beginning to end, because there was the evidence of Mr. La- bouchere and Mr. Brunner of what took place at that meeting. They must not accept Government statements of what took place in Ireland. He—and he was a magistrate for the county of Lancaster— did not hesitate to say that those policemen who shot three innocent men were guilty of wilful mur- der. (Hear, hear.) And Mr. Balfour would not even have an inquiry made. ("Shame.") But they could not prevent an inquest being held, and he was thankful that the English people had an opportunity of reading the evidence given at that coroner's inquiry. He trusted and he believed that the day was very near when Ireland would have what she wanted—her own measure of Home Rule. When Ireland got that there would be an end of the National League, there would be freedom and jus- tice throughout the land, and the people would be contented and happy. Mr. Brunner told him that he never saw people so easily controlled, and so easily managed, as were the people at these large meetings when they were spoken to with kindness and with sympathy. But the Tory Government by the measure they had introduced were trying`to

He might be there ; but if he wanted a reward, or a degree, the rules of the university came into force, and he was prevented taking de- grees. I have mentioned several instance in which there have been changes, as I think for the better, in the Established Church, and in certain things re- lating to it. But I wish to say, notwithstanding those changes which have done something to diminish the prestige of the Established Church, I should think that at the present time the Episcopalian body is doing as much good as ever it I did in the repression of error and ignorance. Ido not think that it will be challenged that the Estab- lished Church, notwithstanding what has been done to diminish its prestige, is as useful as it ever was before. (Hear, hear.) I hope that in the great question that you will have to settle during this generation the people belonging to the Established Church may realise that fact, and that they may be- come helpers with you in bringing before the people of this country the fact, as you will do, that State patronage, and State control, of religion, are evils. (Cheers.) When the Church thinks proper to go in her own strength in the great contest against ignorance and error, she will do so with double vigour and with double success. (Cheers.) It is not necessary for me to notice recent events, but I may just say that it is only twenty years ago since the Irish Church was disestablished, and an end was put to a great injustice by which a particular sect I enjoyed all the patronage and all the incomes of the Church there, only one-sixth of the people of that country belonging to that sect. Now, I have avoided matters of controversy, and have stated ' facts. Ido not want to enter into any controversy to-night. You know what my opinions are. (Cheers.) You know perfectly well what I think of all these changes. You know that I appro ie of them, but I am not going to defend them to-night. There is a great deal yet to be done, and you will have to do it. We who are advanced in life have done, I daresay, what we could—(cheers)—but you, especially the younger of you, have a gread deal to do, and I hope the time is coming when, if you have not already resolved to do it, you will so resolve. What people in your position and mine can individually do is not very great. Our means of usefulness, and our influence, are not great, but they are something, and we have numbers on our side. A grain of sand is only a very little thing, and yet a number of grains of sand bind and con- fine the mighty oc3an, and maintain the earth in existence, and so it is that while our individual effort may be mean and contemptible, united to- gether we can do very much indeed. (Cheers.) It would be a great mistake if anybody in this room were to believe that because he can do little he should not trouble to do anything. The plan is to do your best. (Cheers.) That you are responsible for, but you are not responsible for any more. Perhaps you may receive some encouragement from the re- collection that there was once a woman who cast two mites into the treasury, and for doing this she received this commendation from lips whose com- mendation was better than life—" She bath done what she could." (Continued cheers.) The following gentlemen were then elected to at- tend the National Liberal Federation Conference at Nottingham in October next as delegates from the association :—Mr. G. Rylands, Mr. J. Platt, Mr. F. A. Roberts, Alderman Burgess, and Alderman John Crosfield.

Mr. JOHN WALKER, in proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman, mentioned that in looking over a newspaper file for the year 1853, he had come across the names both of Mr. McMinnies and of Mr. Bur- gess as hard workers together. The resolution was seconded, and carried with applause. At the conclusion of the meeting Mr. H. WHIT- Him said that he thought more opportunity should have been given to those present to express their appreciation of the services rendered by Mr. Mc- Minnies, and the CHAtnatAN explained that the proper time, had they taken advantage of it, to do so was when Mr. Crosfield had presented the address, and before Mr. McMinnies replied. Mr. Mc- Minnies's state of health was such, he also ex- plained, as to make it inadvisable to have a lengthy meeting. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: RP LIGIOUS MANIA•
div.p: RP LIGIOUS MANIA•

On Wednesday morning, at the county t'etty Sessions, at Warrington, John Cawley, a farmer, ot Rixton, was summoned by his wife, Nancy Cawley, who lives at Cadishead, and who alleged that her husband assaulted her on the 12th instant.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant and Mr. P. Davies for the defendant.—Addressing the Bench, Mr. Browne said that this was the old, old tale of Cawley v Cawley, but on this occasion it had as- sumed a more serious nature. On Monday week his client, who lived apart from her husband under a deed of separation, went to the defendant's house to get some butter. She did not go into the house, but when in the lane asked the son to get her the butter. He was, however, forbidden by his father to supply her, and immediately afterwards the father himself came out, carrying a gallon can, which he took to the pump. He filled the can with water, which he threw over his wife, and having repeated this performance thirteen times, he then struck her in the face with the can. Complainant, in her evidence, bore out this statement, and added that she put her umbrella up when her husband was deluaing her with water. (Laughter.) Questioned by Mr. Davies as to the deed of separa- tion, she exclaimed "He might well not have his wife at home when he has his old sweetheart with him."—Mr. Davies: Were you shouting "Glory, glory, hallelujah ?" No, I was not. I said "It is glory and tribulation." I gloried in the water.—Did not you defy him, put up your umbrella, and say "Throw away as much as you like?" No; I said something about tiring him out. "I can stand the storm, it won't be long; and we shall anchor by and bye." My husband has no mercy; he threw me into prison for doing right, and he may be in prison himself some day. I did right and he did wrong; in the sight of God, anyhow.-1N hat was the book you had? "Good Words."—Do you take "Good Words" every time you go for butter? Yes: Ido not like bad words. I went to do my duty,and , to give inN daughter good advice—to come to the I Salvation Army.—Did not you employ a number of men to burn an effigy before his house? No.—Did not you say to those blackguards of men "If you do not do as I tell you I shall neither give you gold nor silver? No; they were little boys, and I did not bring them there. It was not my ordering, but they only served him and his woman right.—After further cross-examination Mr. Davies said that the complainant suffered from religious mania, and seemed in consequence to be, in a slight way, demented. Defendant found it im- possible to live with her, and a deed of separation was drawn up at the suggestion ot the magistrates. She had since, against the terms of the agreement, persistently annoyed her husband, and was in the habit of singing Salvation Army songs in front of the door of his house.—Mr. P. Stubs, who presided, after a consultation with his colleague on the bench, Mr. Z. Armitage said that there was no doubt about an assault having been committed, but the defendant seemed to have entirely disregarded the agreement. She had most improperly and wickedly given provocation, and there was no , religion about the course she had taken. Under the circumstances a fine of is and costs only would be inflicted on the defendant.

Taw SHEFFIELD ACCIDENT. -- The inquest was resumed at Sheffield, on Wednesday, into the death of . the nine workmen killed at Messrs. Vickers, eons, and Co.'s works, Sheffield. The jury found that the explosion was cimsed by molten steel coming in contact with water, but there was not sufficient evidence to justify them in declaring the actual cause. EXPLOSION AT A CHEMICAL WORES.—On Thursday an explosion occurred at the works of Messrs. Brown and Co., chemical manufacturers, Dewsbury. The foreman noticing one of the stills, which was filled with boiling tar, was leaking, attempted to draw the material off by applying a shovel full of fire to the tap attached to the still. The blaze c ime in contact with inflammable oil from a cooler boiler, and the loud crash which followed could be heard miles around. Two men were injured, one seriously.
At Lambeth Police Court, on Friday afternoon, In the Gambling Club case, Runt, the proprietor of the club, was sentenced to six months' hard labour.

It is stated that several cases of cholera are occurring daily in Rome. The disease, however. is of a mild form, and almost confined to the poorer classes. The result of the ballot among the Northumberland miners upon the question of paying their direct representa- tives in Parliament was &dared on Friday ; 3,387 have voted for payment, and 4.800 against. MYSTEBIOUS DEATHS Flto3l POISONING —A mysterious poisoning case occurred on Thursday evening at Camberley, Surrey. Hannah rowels and her son Edward partook of supper at nine o'clock, and at 10-45 they died, death being attributed to poisoning. The police have seized some jam and aotibilious pills. Two WOMEN BURNED TO Datcrs.—Two women, Mrs Frost, aged 38, and Sarah Eimmonds, 35, died e the Bristol Infirmary on Friday morning from the effests of burns caused, it is supposed, by the bursting of a paraffin lamp. The women were discovered in their house fright- fully burnt about the head, arms, and body. The remains of a paraffin lamp were found about the room, and it is surmised that the lamp had explothd.

EXECUTION FOR MURDERING SIXTEEN PERSONS. A Central News telegram dated Vienna, Friday, states : The brigand chief AtbanasOff, was executed at Sofia yester- day, the murder of no fewer than sixteen persons having been proved against him. Fresh bands of brigands are ap- pearing in the neighbourhood of Dubnitzs.

div.head: . A TOWN ON FIRE.
div.p: . A TOWN ON FIRE.

TORONTO, FRIDAY. 8 A.sr.—A terrible fire is raging at I Graven Hurst, Ontario, threatening the total destruction of the place. As the means at the disposal of the townspeople are altogether inadequate to check the progress of the flames, which are spreading rapidly, assistance has been despatched to Graven Hurst, and it is hoped that by its speedy arrival a portion of the town may be saved. A num. ber of buildings, including a hotel and a foundry, have already been destroyed. The origin of the fire is un. known.

div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. -- 111110 M OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C.

Tbe Stock Market during the first half of the week was subject to one of those fits of depression which are begot by falling markets and absence of business. The heavy fall in Mexican rails has been due not to speculative market riggers, but to sales by boncp.fide holders of stock, which realise that the Central will be able to do what has long been feared but not recognised. The future improvement In Mexican rails is very problematical. So hopeless does this improvement appear at present, that holders should lose no time in gett.rig but of them at the very first op- portunity. On Thursday Americans experienced one of those sudden jumps which are characteristic of those stocks, and the re. bound is often just as great. The absence of general sup- port to the market prevents any very sustained effort in sending up prices. Home rails have been a fist market, especially in southern Hues. Speculators in those stocks may expect continued decline In traffics of both Brighton and Dover, as with an accompanying fall in prices, there was a slight improve- ment in both these stocks on Thursday. But from causes mentioned above the " bears " will have the best of it for the next few weeks.

The number of companies that are every week being wound op forms a melancholy record of our time, undoubted successes according to the glowing prospects of the promo- ter turning out miserable failuresovith loss, and often ruin to unfortunate shareholders, who have ne remedy against the people who have deceived them. Tne traffic receipts of the Grand Trunk Railway Corn. pany, of Canada, for the week ending the 17th met, show an increase of £7,379; those of the Chicago and Grand Trunk Co., an increase of £2,153. The aggregate for twelve weeks to above date shows an increase in the Grand Trunk Com- pany's receipts of £62,031 ; an increase in the Chicago and Grand Trunk Company's of £16,580 ; a decrease in the Detroit Grand lintel and Milwaukie Co. of £4,049. The traffic receipts of the Hull, Barnsley, and West Rid- ing Junction Railway and Dock Co. for the week ending 18th September, amount to £4,369 ; being an increase of £907.

div.head: FRODSH AM.
div.p: FRODSH AM.

HARVEST TIUNICSOIVING SERVICES.—In connection with Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsham, tha annual harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday morning and evening. The sacred edifice was tastefully decorated with flowers, fruit, and cereals. The preacher was the recently appointed minister of the circuit. The choir sang several anthems. The collections, amounting to £6 13, were in aid of the circuit fund.

div.head: FUNERAL OF LADY HOPWOOD.
div.p: FUNERAL OF LADY HOPWOOD.

The mortal remains of the late Lady Ellinor Hop- wood, wife of the Rector of Winwick, were on Saturday morning interred in the grave-yard at Winwick Church. Although it had been intimated that the funeral would be of a private character, a considerable number of people, principally gentry and farmers of the neighbourhood, attended as a mark of respect to the memory of the deceased lady. Shortly before eleven o'clock the funeral procession left the late residence of the deceased, Winwick Hall. The carriage in front was occupied by Dr. White, the medical attendant of Lady Hop- wood, and next came the hearse. A carriage which followed contained the husband of the deceased, the Rev. Canon Hopwood, Mrs Darby (wife of the Dean of Chester), and Miss Hopwood (husband and daughters of the deceased), and Mrs A. Hopwood, daughter-in-law. Next, walking, came the Rev. Frank E. Hopwood and the Earl of Derby (son and nephew of the deceased), Major A. H. Hopwood and Mr. C. A. Hopwood, priN ate secretary to the Mar- quis of Salisbury (sons 0, deceased), Lord Stanley of Preston and Rev. E. P. Stanley (nephews), Cap- tain Stanley and Mr. Leycester Stanley (nephews), and the Von. Archdeacon Hornby and the Dean of Chester. Six maidservants, also walking two deep, followed, the butler and footman bringing up the rear. The procession was met at the churchyard by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, nephew of the de- ceased, and the Rev. J.Carson, (curate of Winwick), and as it entered the church Mr. James Kerfoot, the organist, played the "Dead March" in "Saul." The psalms and lessons were read by Canon Penrhyn. Mr. Kerfoot played Dr. Boyce's "Funeral March" as the coffin was borne from the church, and at the grave the burial service was read by Canon Penrhyn. A large number of wreaths had been forwarded by friends, including Viscount and Lady Down, Mr. and Mrs. Begot, of Sheen, Surrey; Lady Emma Tal- bot, Miss Hornby, of Daulton ; Mrs. T. J. Gillespie, Newton; from the Clergy Daughters' School, War- rington, and others. Amongst those present at the interment were—Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, S. Wilkin- son, H. Monk, R. Smith, and E. J. Hack; Messrs. T. Comber, J.P., Myddleton Hall; George Comber, Chester; J. Swinton, Thomas Stone, R. -Stone, J. R. Worsley, P. Longton, W. Wright, Alderroot Farm; James Warburton, Dallam ; W. Pennington, Thomas Shaw, Hermitage Green; G. Powlson, E. C. Cooper, G. C. Gilroy (Winwick Grammar School), J. W. Pen- nington, R. H. Carson, R. Clarke, and a number of parishioners and members of the congregation. The coffin was a massive oak one, with deep oak mould- ings and ebony panels, and was fitted with klieg continuous mountings, the lid being of ebony with oak mouldings. Tke shield bore the following in- scription :—" Ellinor Mary Hopwood, born 3rd May, 1807; died 11th September, 1887." Messrs. S. E. and R. Johnson, Warrington, had charge of the funeral arrangements.
